tasks.name: CVRP X-n1001-k43
tasks.description: Route identical vehicles of capacity 131 from one depot to serve the 1000 customers of the CVRPLIB X-set instance X-n1001-k43. Every customer is visited exactly once, the total demand on a route may not exceed the capacity, and every route starts and ends at the depot. The number of routes is free (the k in the instance name does not limit it). Minimise the total cost: the sum over all routes of the Euclidean distances between consecutive stops, the legs from and to the depot included, each distance rounded to the nearest integer.
tasks.contract: solve(inst) -> list of routes; a route is a list of customer ids from 1 to n in visiting order (the depot is node 0 and is not listed; empty routes are ignored). inst is a dict with n (number of customers), capacity, coords (array of shape (n + 1, 2), row 0 is the depot), demand (integer array of length n + 1, demand[0] = 0) and name. Score: the total cost, minimized.

tasks.contract: construct() -> list of distinct strings of length 19 over the capital letters A, C, G, T (at least one word and at most 20000; a longer list is invalid). Score: number of words, maximized.

limitations: The record is the proven maximum: by the Plotkin bound a code over {A, C, G, T} of length 20 and distance 16 has at most 16 words, and a reverse-complement code C gives the code C together with the reverse complements of its words, of twice its size, so nothing can beat it; a result can only match it.

The record is the lower bound of Aboluion, Smith and Perkins, Discrete Mathematics 312 (2012), marked there as a new best known result (also the 2011 PhD thesis of Aboluion). The codeword file of the archive named in the paper is replayed word by word through this task's verifier. The codes of these authors have only even GC weights, so for some cells the weight is not floor(n/2); the task lets the code choose its weight. The values are algebraic constructions (cyclic additive codes, cosets, shortening): a plain search reaches 62 to 85% of them (REVIEW.md, section 21). The tables of Montemanni, Smith and Koul (2014) show no larger value.
Only open entries with a bound of at most 2000 words in the table are tasks, so that the pairwise check stays cheap.
The record was reproduced by this task's verifier from a published solution (or an optimiser run). See VALIDITY.md.

tasks.name: EPFL adder, LUT-6 levels
tasks.description: Optimise the EPFL combinational benchmark circuit adder (adds two 128-bit numbers; 256 inputs, 129 outputs) with the logic-synthesis tool ABC and map it to lookup tables (LUTs) with at most 6 inputs, minimising the number of LUT levels, the largest number of LUTs on a path from an input to an output. The result must compute the same function as the original circuit.
tasks.contract: script() -> string of ABC commands separated by `;` or newlines. The evaluator runs `read <circuit>; <script>` in ABC and writes out the network the script leaves. That network must consist only of LUTs with at most 6 inputs (in ABC a LUT mapper such as `if -K 6` produces one; library gates or a wider node are invalid), and it must be equivalent to the original circuit, which a separate ABC process checks with `cec`. The script may not contain the characters ! / \ ~, may not use commands that read or write files, change the session or start other programs (read*, write*, load*, dump*, save* and their short forms, source, alias, set, unset, history, cd, ls, pwd, quit, exit), and may not ask for LUTs wider than 6 inputs (-K above 6). Time limits: 1200 s for the script, 900 s for the equivalence check. A script that is refused, fails, runs out of time or changes the function is invalid. Score: the largest number of LUTs with two or more inputs on a path from an input to an output (buffers, inverters and constants are not counted), minimized.

tasks.name: DC3 Convex QP
tasks.description: DC3 Convex QP
tasks.contract: solve(problem, time_limit) -> x: a length-problem['n'] vector for the instance dict (kind, form in {qp, qcqp, socp, lp, milp}, arrays Q, p, A, b, G, h, lb, ub, and H/g/r, cones, c, A_ub, b_ub, A_eq, b_eq, integer as applicable; nonconvex instances add sum(sin(x)), nonsmooth ones add 0.5*||x||_1 to the objective). l2o.objective(problem, x), l2o.violation(problem, x) and l2o.scipy_constraints(problem) are available. Score: mean over five seeded instances of the relative optimality gap against an independent reference (Clarabel / HiGHS / multistart SLSQP); infeasible (violation > 1e-4), non-finite or over-time solutions count as gap 1. Lower is better.

tasks.name: Narrow admissible tuple
tasks.description: Construct the largest admissible tuple within [0, 5000] by selecting a removed residue class for each prime. This is the fixed-diameter maximization formulation actually benchmarked in paper Table 2.
tasks.contract: construct() -> list of distinct integers in [0, n] forming an admissible tuple: for every prime p <= len(tuple) some residue class mod p is missed (FunSearch fixed-diameter formulation). Score: tuple size

sources.locator: Section 3, Tables 1-3
examples/nat_spec.py

limitations: Execution interface inspected in pinned source. Full paper experiments have not been reproduced here.

The source itself uses a fixed diameter bound n=5000 and maximizes surviving tuple size. The local constructor directly returns integers in [0,5000]; for k distinct values it checks a missing residue for every prime<=k (larger primes cannot be fully occupied). The source instead evolves a prime-residue sieve priority. The mathematical feasible set/size objective are shared but candidate interface and search differ. MCTS-AHD ternary admissible sets are a different task and have been restored separately.

tasks.name: Max-cut, G-set G1
tasks.description: Partition the 800 vertices of the G-set graph G1 into two sides so that the total weight of the edges whose endpoints are on different sides is as large as possible (max-cut). The graph is undirected and has 19176 edges, each given once; every edge has weight 1.
tasks.contract: solve(n, edges) -> sequence of n integers, each 0 or 1: the side of every vertex. edges is an int64 array with one row (i, j, w) per edge, vertices numbered from 0. Score: total weight of the edges whose endpoints are on different sides, maximized.

sources.locator: G1
2025 report of G81 14060 and related cuts
An Application of Combinatorial Optimization to Statistical Physics and Circuit Layout Design
Improved approximation algorithms for maximum cut and satisfiability problems using semidefinite programming
Rank-Two Relaxation Heuristics for MAX-CUT and Other Binary Quadratic Programs
Breakout Local Search for the Max-Cutproblem

Helmberg and Rendl (2000), A Spectral Bundle Method for Semidefinite Programming (title per Crossref): a semidefinite programming method, not a max-cut paper; the brief credits it with the first use of the G-set, which was not checked.

Khan and Shukla (2025), New Best-Known Max-Cut Solution for the G63 Instance in the G-Set Benchmark: describes the set as random, toroidal and planar graphs with 1 or +-1 weights, and gives the earlier best value for G63.

limitations: Specialised solvers (breakout local search, simulated bifurcation, GES-PR) are strong on this set.

The graph is undirected and has 4000 edges, each given once; every edge has weight 1 or -1, and an edge of weight -1 that is cut lowers the total.
tasks.contract: solve(n, edges) -> sequence of n integers, each 0 or 1: the side of every vertex. edges is an int64 array with one row (i, j, w) per edge, vertices numbered from 0. Score: total weight of the edges whose endpoints are on different sides, maximized.

sources.locator: 2025 report of G81 14060 and related cuts
An Application of Combinatorial Optimization to Statistical Physics and Circuit Layout Design
Improved approximation algorithms for maximum cut and satisfiability problems using semidefinite programming
Rank-Two Relaxation Heuristics for MAX-CUT and Other Binary Quadratic Programs
Breakout Local Search for the Max-Cutproblem

Helmberg and Rendl (2000), A Spectral Bundle Method for Semidefinite Programming (title per Crossref): a semidefinite programming method, not a max-cut paper; the brief credits it with the first use of the G-set, which was not checked.

Khan and Shukla (2025), New Best-Known Max-Cut Solution for the G63 Instance in the G-Set Benchmark: describes the set as random, toroidal and planar graphs with 1 or +-1 weights, and gives the earlier best value for G63.

limitations: Specialised solvers (breakout local search, simulated bifurcation, GES-PR) are strong on this set.

tasks.name: Job-shop scheduling dmu11
tasks.description: Schedule 30 jobs on 15 machines (job-shop benchmark instance dmu11). Every job is a sequence of 15 operations, one on each machine, that must run in the given order; an operation occupies its machine for its whole duration without interruption, and a machine processes one operation at a time. Minimise the makespan, the time at which the last operation ends.
tasks.contract: solve(inst) -> starts, a list of n_jobs lists of non-negative integers: starts[j][k] is the start time of operation k of job j. inst has name, n_jobs, n_machines and jobs[j] = list of (machine, duration) pairs in processing order, machines numbered from 0. Operation k + 1 of a job may not start before operation k has ended, and two operations on one machine may not overlap (one may start at the moment the other ends). Score: the makespan, minimized.

Every job is a sequence of 15 operations, one on each machine, that must run in the given order; an operation occupies its machine for its whole duration without interruption, and a machine processes one operation at a time. Minimise the makespan, the time at which the last operation ends.
tasks.contract: solve(inst) -> starts, a list of n_jobs lists of non-negative integers: starts[j][k] is the start time of operation k of job j. inst has name, n_jobs, n_machines and jobs[j] = list of (machine, duration) pairs in processing order, machines numbered from 0. Operation k + 1 of a job may not start before operation k has ended, and two operations on one machine may not overlap (one may start at the moment the other ends). Score: the makespan, minimized.

tasks.name: Stable Diffusion excess blue
tasks.description: Optimize a text prompt to increase excess blue in a complete SD1.4-generated image.
tasks.contract: candidate() -> str (at most 4096 UTF-8 bytes; SD tokenizer retains its native 77-token limit). The grader renders one full 512x512 RGB image with fixed SD1.4 fp16/10 steps/seed 99 and maximizes the selected channel sum minus half each other channel sum.

sources.locator: Section 4.4 and Appendix D
scripts/stablediffusion.py

limitations: Arena initialization is the shared neutral prompt A photograph of a landscape. It replaces a non-executable placeholder and does not reproduce the paper's sampled human-prompt population or 5000-evaluation search protocol.

Guidance 7.5, negative_prompt=None, one image, PNDM scheduler from pinned checkpoint, legacy AttnProcessor, disabled TF32, deterministic cuDNN settings and modern pinned package versions are explicit Arena protocol choices. Published paper scores are not comparable by default.

Candidate Python runs in a separate child with 3 CPU seconds, 512 MiB address-space, 5-second wall and 32 KiB output bounds; only a bounded UTF-8 prompt string is accepted. Parent verifies readonly model files and initializes its pipeline after the child exits. A same-UID container is not an adversarial secrecy boundary.
A pinned GPU runtime and complete model assets are required; production GPU admission and fresh canonical readiness remain separate from private seed probes.

tasks.name: MIPLIB 2017 open instance allcolor58
tasks.description: Find a feasible solution of the MIPLIB 2017 instance allcolor58 with as low an objective value as possible (a maximisation model is negated, so that lower is better for every instance). A solution is feasible when every variable bound, every row bound and the integrality of every integer variable hold within an absolute tolerance of 1e-6 on the values as they are returned; integer variables are not rounded first.
tasks.contract: solve(model) -> numpy array of num_cols values, one per column. model has name, mps_path (the uncompressed MPS file), num_cols, num_rows, A (scipy CSR matrix of the rows), col_cost, col_lower, col_upper, row_lower, row_upper, integrality (bool array), offset, maximise and indicators (a list of (row, column, value): such a row has to hold only when that column equals the value; empty for most instances). Score: col_cost @ x + offset in minimisation form (negated when maximise is true), minimized; an infeasible vector is invalid.

sources.locator: allcolor58
Mixed-integer linear programming heuristics for the prepack optimization problem
Gleixner et al. (2021), MIPLIB 2017: data-driven compilation of the 6th mixed-integer programming library (benchmark paper, not evidence).
Instance pages with submitter, group, status and best known objective.

limitations: The objective listed on the open-instances page may have been improved since 2026-11-11 (the list did not change between 2026-11-02 and 2026-11-11).
Candidates may call HiGHS through highspy; a stronger solver is a method, not a discovery by the workflow.

A solution is feasible when every variable bound, every row bound and the integrality of every integer variable hold within an absolute tolerance of 1e-6 on the values as they are returned; integer variables are not rounded first.
tasks.contract: solve(model) -> numpy array of num_cols values, one per column. model has name, mps_path (the uncompressed MPS file), num_cols, num_rows, A (scipy CSR matrix of the rows), col_cost, col_lower, col_upper, row_lower, row_upper, integrality (bool array), offset, maximise and indicators (a list of (row, column, value): such a row has to hold only when that column equals the value; empty for most instances). Score: col_cost @ x + offset in minimisation form (negated when maximise is true), minimized; an infeasible vector is invalid.

tasks.name: MIPLIB 2017 open instance xmas10
tasks.description: Find a feasible solution of the MIPLIB 2017 instance xmas10 with as low an objective value as possible (a maximisation model is negated, so that lower is better for every instance). A solution is feasible when every variable bound, every row bound and the integrality of every integer variable hold within an absolute tolerance of 1e-6 on the values as they are returned; integer variables are not rounded first.
tasks.contract: solve(model) -> numpy array of num_cols values, one per column. model has name, mps_path (the uncompressed MPS file), num_cols, num_rows, A (scipy CSR matrix of the rows), col_cost, col_lower, col_upper, row_lower, row_upper, integrality (bool array), offset, maximise and indicators (a list of (row, column, value): such a row has to hold only when that column equals the value; empty for most instances). Score: col_cost @ x + offset in minimisation form (negated when maximise is true), minimized; an infeasible vector is invalid.

tasks.name: Quadratic assignment, QAPLIB sko100a
tasks.description: Quadratic assignment problem, QAPLIB instance sko100a: given two 100 x 100 integer matrices a and b, find a permutation p of 0..99 that minimises the cost, the sum over all i and j of a[i, j] * b[p[i], p[j]]. In the usual reading one matrix holds the flows between facilities and the other the distances between locations, and p assigns the one to the other; the cost formula is what is scored.
tasks.contract: solve(a, b) -> permutation p of 0..n-1 (a list of n integers, each exactly once). a and b are the first and second matrix of the QAPLIB file (int64 arrays of shape (n, n), passed as copies). Score: the exact integer cost, the sum over all i and j of a[i, j] * b[p[i], p[j]], minimized.

tasks.name: Quadratic assignment, QAPLIB tai150b
tasks.description: Quadratic assignment problem, QAPLIB instance tai150b: given two 150 x 150 integer matrices a and b, find a permutation p of 0..149 that minimises the cost, the sum over all i and j of a[i, j] * b[p[i], p[j]]. In the usual reading one matrix holds the flows between facilities and the other the distances between locations, and p assigns the one to the other; the cost formula is what is scored.
tasks.contract: solve(a, b) -> permutation p of 0..n-1 (a list of n integers, each exactly once). a and b are the first and second matrix of the QAPLIB file (int64 arrays of shape (n, n), passed as copies). Score: the exact integer cost, the sum over all i and j of a[i, j] * b[p[i], p[j]], minimized.

tasks.name: Biology: protein multiple-alignment accuracy on BAliBASE reference alignments
tasks.description: Align the unaligned protein sequences of 26 BAliBASE reference-1 test cases, spanning very divergent and medium-divergence families. The evaluator checks that each alignment is a valid gapped version of the input sequences and scores the sum-of-pairs agreement with the structure-based reference alignment on its annotated core blocks.
tasks.contract: align(sequences) -> list of aligned rows, one per input sequence, all of the same length (at most 6 times the longest input sequence plus 10 columns), each row equal to its input sequence with '-' gap characters inserted (upper-case amino acids). sequences is a list of 4 to 10 unaligned protein sequences of a BAliBASE reference-1 test case. align is called once per test case in a sandboxed subprocess with a 240 s CPU budget for all 26 cases. Score (maximize): mean sum-of-pairs score over the cases, i.e. the fraction of residue pairs that the structure-based reference alignment places in the same core-block column and the candidate also aligns; the total-column score is reported alongside

sources.locator: Thompson, Plewniak and Poch (1999): comparison of multiple alignment programs on reference alignments; defines the sum-of-pairs and total-column scores on core blocks implemented here.
Thompson, Koehl, Ripp and Poch (2005): BAliBASE 3.0, the structure-based reference alignments and core-block annotations used as ground truth.
Katoh et al. (2002), MAFFT: an alignment method whose main goal is accurate and fast multiple sequence alignment, the problem this task scores.
BAliBASE download page; the archive BAliBASE_R1-5.tar.gz (reference sets RV11 and RV12 of this task) states no licence and is downloaded by the prepare script rather than redistributed.

limitations: Only 26 of the 82 reference-1 cases are used (at most 10 sequences and 300 reference columns each, and at least 43 core-block columns; ten further cases within the size limits, each with fewer than 40 core-block columns, are not used) so that a CPU-only aligner finishes within the budget; averages are therefore not comparable with published whole-benchmark numbers.

SP and TC are an independent implementation of the published definitions restricted to core blocks; it scores the reference alignments at exactly 1.0 but is not byte-compatible with the bundled bali_score program.
Reference alignments are themselves structure-based estimates of homology, and core blocks cover only part of each alignment.
The references are public, so search feedback can overfit this fixed subset; a candidate aligner should be checked on held-out families before any claim of improved accuracy.

tasks.name: Biology: HP lattice protein folding on the square lattice
tasks.description: Fold the ten standard two-dimensional HP benchmark sequences (20 to 100 residues) into low-energy self-avoiding conformations on the square lattice. The evaluator checks self-avoidance, recomputes the hydrophobic contact energy of every conformation and scores the mean ratio to the lowest energies reported in the literature.
tasks.contract: fold(sequence, dimension) -> list of len(sequence) integer lattice points (lists of length dimension). sequence is a string of H and P residues; dimension is 2 (square lattice). The returned walk must be self-avoiding with unit steps between consecutive residues. Energy = minus the number of H-H pairs on neighbouring lattice sites that are not adjacent along the chain; the evaluator recomputes it. fold is called once per benchmark sequence in a sandboxed subprocess with a 120 s CPU budget for all sequences together. Score (maximize): mean over the 10 benchmark sequences of energy / best_known_energy (both energies are negative), so 0 is an unfolded chain, 1.0 reproduces every best-known energy and a value above 1.0 beats one

sources.locator: Lau and Dill (1989) define the HP lattice model of protein folding whose minimum-energy conformations this task searches for.

Kou, Oh and Wong (2006), Tables IV and V: the nine widely used 2D benchmark sequences and the lowest energies reached by equi-energy sampling, genetic algorithms, evolutionary Monte Carlo, PERM, SISPER and human-guided search.
Zhang, Kou and Liu (2007), Tables II and III: the benchmark sequences longer than 50 residues and the fragment-regrowth energies used here as best-known values.
Wuest and Landau (2012), Table II: Wang-Landau sampling reaches the same putative ground-state energies for the long 2D chains (-42, -53, -48, -50).

limitations: The HP model is a coarse two-letter abstraction of a protein: its ground states are not real protein structures, and a better HP energy is a better solution of the stated lattice optimisation problem rather than a structural-biology result.

Best-known energies for these 2D sequences are the lowest values reported in the cited literature, not proven optima, except for the 25-residue chain, whose -8 equals the parity upper bound on contacts (H-H contacts join residues of opposite parity, and its four H residues at positions 6, 12, 18 and 24 have two free neighbour sites each); the evaluator cannot certify optimality, only recompute energies.
All ten sequences share one CPU budget inside the sandboxed subprocess, so the score depends on that budget and is not comparable with the multi-hour searches of the cited papers.
The published energies are embedded in the evaluator as reference values only; the candidate never receives them.
provenance.benchmark: Biology: HP lattice protein folding on the square lattice
provenance.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

Score (maximize): mean over the 16 benchmark sequences of energy / best_known_energy (both energies are negative), so 0 is an unfolded chain, 1.0 reproduces every best-known energy and a value above 1.0 beats one

sources.locator: Lau and Dill (1989) define the HP lattice model whose cubic-lattice ground states this task searches for.
Yue, Fiebig, Thomas, Chan, Shakhnovich and Dill (1995) introduce the ten 48-residue cubic-lattice sequences and determine their ground states by constraint-based hydrophobic-core construction.
Bachmann and Janke (2004), Table II: the ten 48-mer sequences in run-length notation with their ground-state energies (-32, -34, -34, -33, -32, -32, -32, -31, -34, -33) and degeneracies.

tasks.name: Biology: probabilistic forecasts of state influenza hospital admissions
tasks.description: Issue weekly quantile forecasts of laboratory-confirmed influenza hospital admissions one to four weeks ahead for every US state through the held-out 2024-2025 season, seeing only the surveillance history up to each forecast week. The evaluator scores the quantiles with the weighted interval score used by the CDC FluSight hub.
tasks.contract: forecast(history, reference_date, quantiles, horizons) -> dict mapping every location code of history to a 4 x 23 list of predictive quantiles (rows = horizons 1..4 weeks ahead, columns = the 23 FluSight quantile levels, non-negative and non-decreasing along each row). history maps location codes ('US' plus the two-digit FIPS codes of the 50 states, DC and Puerto Rico) to the weekly admission counts up to and including the week ending on reference_date (None where the hub reports no value). forecast is called once per reference date, in chronological order, inside a sandboxed subprocess that never sees later weeks, with a 180 s CPU budget for the whole season. Score (minimize): mean weighted interval score (Bracher et al. 2021) over the 26 reference dates of the 2024-2025 season, the 52 state-level locations and the four horizons; the US aggregate is not scored

sources.locator: Mathis et al. (2024): evaluation of the FluSight collaborative forecasts of laboratory-confirmed influenza hospital admissions, the exact target, horizons and WIS metric used here.
Reich et al. (2019): multiyear, multimodel assessment of seasonal influenza forecasting in the United States, establishing the forecasting problem and its evaluation.
Bracher, Ray, Gneiting and Reich (2021): definition of the weighted interval score for quantile-format epidemic forecasts, implemented independently in the evaluator.
FluSight forecast hub (MIT licence): target-data/target-hospital-admissions.csv provides the weekly state-level admission counts from CDC NHSN used for training and verification.

limitations: Training history and verification both use the latest published snapshot, not the data vintages available in real time, so reporting revisions and backfill are not modelled and the task is easier than the live challenge.
Only the hospital-admission target, four horizons and the November-April window are scored; the hub's rate-change and seasonal targets are not.
The score is the mean weighted interval score in admissions, so it is dominated by populous states and is not comparable with the hub's relative-WIS leaderboard.
The held-out season is public, so search feedback on this fixed split can overfit it; a candidate should be frozen and tested on a later season before any claim of forecasting skill.
A better score is a better statistical forecaster on these seasons, not an epidemiological discovery.

tasks.name: Biology: phylogenetic topology recovery from simulated sequences
tasks.description: Reconstruct the unrooted tree topology of twenty simulated instances with 8 to 32 taxa and 250 to 2000 sites, generated inside the evaluator under the Jukes-Cantor model with hidden random topologies and branch lengths. The score is the mean normalized Robinson-Foulds distance to the generating trees.
tasks.contract: reconstruct(sequences) -> Newick string over the labels t0..t(n-1) (branch lengths optional, trailing semicolon optional, every taxon exactly once). sequences maps those labels to equal-length DNA strings over ACGT simulated along an unknown tree. reconstruct is called once per instance in a sandboxed subprocess with a 180 s CPU budget for all 20 instances (8 to 32 taxa, 250 to 2000 sites). Score (minimize): mean normalized Robinson-Foulds distance between the non-trivial unrooted splits of the returned tree and those of the generating tree: the number of splits present in only one of the two trees divided by the total number of splits of both trees (for a binary answer this is RF / (2 (n - 3)); an unresolved star tree scores 1); 0 means recovering every topology exactly

sources.locator: Saitou and Nei (1987): the neighbour-joining method for reconstructing phylogenetic trees, the problem this task scores and the basis of the seed program.
Huelsenbeck (1995), Performance of phylogenetic methods in simulation: evaluating tree-reconstruction accuracy on sequences simulated along known trees, the protocol followed here.
Robinson and Foulds (1981): the split-based tree distance used as the score.
Guindon et al. (2010), PhyML 3.0: maximum-likelihood tree search, the state of practice a candidate would have to match or beat.

limitations: Sequences are simulated under Jukes-Cantor with no rate heterogeneity, no indels and no model misspecification, so the task measures reconstruction under an idealized model rather than on real data.
Instances, topologies and branch-length regimes are a local choice (20 instances, 8 to 32 taxa); results do not transfer automatically to empirical alignments.
Exact recovery is not guaranteed to be attainable from finite data, so the minimum achievable score is unknown and the seed's value is only a baseline.
Branch lengths of the returned tree are ignored: only the unrooted topology is scored.

The simulator, the instance parameters and the seeds are public constants of the evaluator and the sandbox allows numpy, so a candidate that re-implements the generator obtains the generating trees without any inference (such a program scores 0.0). Results are meaningful only for candidates that use the sequences alone, and a claimed method should be confirmed on instances drawn with new seeds.

tasks.name: Lennard-Jones cluster global minimum, 38 atoms
tasks.description: Place 38 atoms interacting through the Lennard-Jones potential (reduced units) to minimise the total energy. LJ38 is the classic hard case of cluster optimisation: the global minimum is a face-centred-cubic truncated octahedron (energy -173.928427, Cambridge Cluster Database) while the icosahedral funnel traps local searches. The evaluator computes the energy exactly; the seed is a cubic lattice fragment.
tasks.contract: construct() -> array of shape (N, 3): Cartesian coordinates of N atoms in reduced Lennard-Jones units (sigma = 1). Atoms must be at least 0.5 apart. Score: total Lennard-Jones energy 4*sum(r^-12 - r^-6) over all pairs, minimized. science_chemistry.relax(positions) (L-BFGS local relaxation) is available to candidates.

sources.locator: Wales and Doye 1997, Global optimization by basin-hopping and the lowest energy structures of Lennard-Jones clusters containing up to 110 atoms.
Cambridge Cluster Database (LJ global minima table, doye.chem.ox.ac.uk/jon/structures/LJ/tables.150.html): N=38, point group Oh, energy -173.928427; inspected 2026-09-20.

limitations: The database values are putative global minima found by extensive searches, not proven optima; the reference is reproduced in tests by constructing the fcc truncated octahedron and relaxing it.
Reaching -173.928427 reproduces a known structure; a lower energy would be a new putative minimum and must be verified independently.

tasks.name: Lowest-energy MMFF94 conformers of eight drug molecules
tasks.description: Find, for each of eight flexible drug molecules, the conformer with the lowest MMFF94 force-field energy while keeping the molecule's connectivity and stereochemistry. The evaluator recomputes the energy of the returned coordinates and compares it with minima from an extensive reference search.
tasks.contract: conformer(molecule) -> array of shape (n_atoms, 3): Cartesian coordinates in Angstrom of every atom, in the atom order of Chem.AddHs(Chem.MolFromSmiles(molecule['smiles'])) (RDKit 2026.03). molecule = {'name', 'smiles', 'atoms' (element symbols in that order), 'formal_charges', 'bonds' ([i, j, bond order])}. Called for eight drugs (imatinib, sildenafil, atorvastatin, oseltamivir, tamoxifen, simvastatin, (S)-verapamil, (R)-ranolazine); all calls together within 300 s, at most 4 threads. The evaluator computes the MMFF94 energy (RDKit, no cutoff, dielectric 1) of exactly the returned coordinates; every bond must lie within 0.70-1.35 times the sum of covalent radii, non-bonded atoms at least 0.6 A apart, and the stereochemistry assigned from the 3D geometry must reproduce the given isomeric SMILES. Score: mean MMFF94 energy above reference minima found by an extensive local search (kcal/mol; minimize; negative = lower)

sources.locator: Pracht, Bohle and Grimme (2020): automated search for low-energy conformers and rotamers (CREST).
Kolossvary and Guida (1996): low-mode search for efficient global conformational analysis.
Riniker and Landrum (2015): ETKDG conformer generation, used by the seed and the reference search.
Halgren (1996): the MMFF94 force field (RDKit implementation used here).
ChEMBL records CHEMBL941, CHEMBL192, CHEMBL1487, CHEMBL1229, CHEMBL83, CHEMBL1064, CHEMBL6966 and CHEMBL1404 for the structures.

limitations: The references are the lowest energies found by this collection's own reference search (ETKDGv3 sampling, MMFF94 minimisation and torsional basin hopping with three or more independent seeds; per-seed results in validation/chemistry-checks.json), not published values and not proven global minima; a negative score means the candidate found lower minima.

MMFF94 in vacuum with a constant dielectric favours intramolecular hydrogen bonds and folded conformers; the force-field minimum is not the bioactive or solution conformer, so the task measures search, not conformational realism.

Atom order and energies depend on the RDKit version (2026.03 here). Verapamil and ranolazine are racemic drugs of which one enantiomer is fixed. The time budget (300 s for all eight molecules) is checked only as a whole.

tasks.name: Morse cluster global minima across the range of the potential
tasks.description: Find the lowest-energy arrangements of 38 to 80 atoms bound by Morse potentials of long, medium and short range (six instances). Energies are recomputed exactly and compared with the putative global minima of Doye and Wales.
tasks.contract: construct(instance) -> array of shape (n, 3): Cartesian coordinates of n atoms in reduced units (pair equilibrium distance 1). instance = {'potential': 'morse', 'rho': range parameter, 'n': atoms}; called once for each of six instances (rho, n) = (3, 80), (6, 38), (6, 75), (10, 38), (10, 50), (10, 80); all six calls together must finish within 300 s (enforced) and should use at most 4 threads (not enforced by the evaluator). The evaluator recomputes E = sum_{i<j} exp(rho(1-r_ij))(exp(rho(1-r_ij)) - 2) (well depth 1); atoms must be at least 0.5 apart. Score: mean over instances of 100*(E - E_pub)/|E_pub| against the putative global minima tabulated by Doye and Wales (1997) (minimize; 0 matches all six, negative is lower than published). chem_clusters.relax(positions, 'morse', rho) and chem_clusters.morse_energy_gradient(positions, rho) may be called

sources.locator: Doye and Wales (1997): Morse potential in reduced units, Table 1 of putative global minima for N <= 80 at rho = 3, 6, 10, 14 (arXiv cond-mat/9709201).
LaTeX source of Table 1, from which the six reference energies (six decimals) were read.

limitations: The references are the 1997 putative minima; the Cambridge Cluster Database listed the same six energies on 2026-11-24, so no later improvement is recorded for these instances, and a score below zero would be a new putative minimum that needs independent confirmation. rho = 14, where later work reported new minima, is not used.

The putative minima are published with coordinates in the database, so a candidate that reproduces remembered structures scores well without searching; scores measure constructions, not search efficiency.
The score averages relative energy excesses (percent of |E|) over six instances with a 300 s budget for all of them; results depend on the machine speed for time-limited searches.

tasks.name: Clique partitions of three fixed split (chordal) graphs
tasks.description: construct() -> three lists of cliques (vertex lists), one per instance from split_graph(n, k, p, seed) for (30,10,0.7,301), (60,20,0.7,302), (90,30,0.7,303) in the verifier: a clique on the first k vertices, an independent set on the rest and each cross pair joined with probability p (split graphs are chordal). Every listed set must be a clique with at least two vertices and every edge must lie in exactly one listed clique. Minimize the total number of cliques; the Erdős-Ordman-Zalcstein question asks whether n^2/6 + O(n) always suffice, and split graphs need at most 3n^2/16 + O(n). The score totals clique partition sizes on three fixed random split graphs; it measures a partitioning method.

tasks.name: Earth science: daily Arctic sea-ice drift from geostrophic winds
tasks.description: Learn how Arctic sea ice drifts in response to the wind from 2000-2014 drifting-buoy tracks and reanalysis sea-level pressure, then predict the daily velocity of every buoy north of 70 N for each day of 2015-2024 from that day's geostrophic wind and the past buoy record. The score is the root-mean-square vector error of the predicted velocities.
tasks.contract: fit_drift_model(training) -> model; model.forecast(history, today) -> float array (n, 2) of the eastward and northward ice velocity (cm/s) of each buoy listed in today over that day (displacement from 00 UTC to 00 UTC of the next day). training and history are dicts of numpy arrays, one row per buoy-day, with day (days since 2000-01-01), buoy (id), lat and lon (00 UTC position, deg; buoys at 70-90 N from the IABP product C), slp_hpa, ug and vg (geostrophic wind, m/s east and north, from a weighted plane fit to NCEP/NCAR daily-mean sea-level pressure within 500 km, air density 1.3) and u, v (the observed velocity, cm/s); training covers 2000-2014. Forecasts are requested in order for every day of 2015-2024 with active buoys; today holds day, buoy, lat, lon, slp_hpa, ug and vg of that day's buoys (the geostrophic wind is the daily mean over the forecast day); history holds all rows of earlier days, including the previous day's velocities, and nothing later. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 240 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: root-mean-square vector error sqrt(mean((u - u_obs)^2 + (v - v_obs)^2)) in cm/s over all 356683 buoy-days; lower is better. Wrong shapes, NaN or values outside [-200, 200] cm/s are invalid

sources.locator: Thorndike and Colony (1982): sea-ice velocity as a linear response to the geostrophic wind (about 1 percent of the wind speed, a few degrees to the right) plus a mean current; the seed and reference use this model.
Rigor, Wallace and Colony (2002): IABP buoy and pressure analyses of Arctic ice motion and its response to atmospheric circulation.
Kalnay et al. (1996): the NCEP/NCAR reanalysis providing the daily-mean sea-level pressure.
IABP product C, interpolated Arctic buoy positions, 2000-2024 (no licence stated; not redistributed; retrieved 2026-10-11).
NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1 daily-mean sea-level pressure, 2000-2024 (public domain).

limitations: The geostrophic wind is computed from 2.5-degree reanalysis pressure by a local plane fit and given for the forecast day itself (a perfect-prognosis forcing); surface winds, ice concentration, thickness and ocean currents are not provided.

Velocities are 24-hour displacements of interpolated buoy positions, so position noise and the interpolation of the product C add error; buoys include ones in the marginal ice zone and in summer, where the free-drift relation is weaker than in the central Arctic.
The number of buoys grows strongly after 2014, so the test years weight recent conditions and regions with dense deployments.
The IABP product states no licence; it is downloaded by the preparation script and not redistributed.
A better score is a better statistical model of ice drift on these buoys, not a scientific discovery; the held-out tracks are public, so search feedback can overfit them.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives positions after the start of a forecast day, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.

tasks.name: Earth science: Gutenberg-Richter b-value from incomplete earthquake catalogues
tasks.description: Estimate the Gutenberg-Richter b-value and the magnitude of completeness of 600 synthetic earthquake catalogues whose small events are missed according to a realistic detection probability. The score is the mean absolute error of the estimated b-values against the generating values.
tasks.contract: estimate_b_and_mc(catalogues) -> float array (600, 2) of [b-value, magnitude of completeness] for each catalogue. catalogues is a list of 600 float arrays of earthquake magnitudes reported in 0.1 bins. Each synthetic catalogue has Gutenberg-Richter magnitudes (b drawn from 0.6-1.4) starting 3 sigma below mu and thinned by the detection probability Phi((m - mu) / sigma) (mu from 0.5-3.0, sigma from 0.05-0.5), with 150-5000 detected events. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 120 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: mean absolute error of b over the 600 catalogues; lower is better. The completeness estimate is compared with the 95 percent detection magnitude mu + 1.645 sigma and reported but not scored. Wrong shapes, NaN, b outside [0.1, 3] or Mc outside [-2, 10] are invalid

sources.locator: Woessner and Wiemer (2005): methods to estimate the magnitude of completeness and their effect on b-value estimates, compared on synthetic and real catalogues; the seed is their maximum-curvature method with the +0.2 correction.
Ogata and Katsura (1993): Gutenberg-Richter magnitudes thinned by a cumulative-normal detection rate, the generating model of the catalogues.

limitations: The catalogues are synthetic: one stationary b-value and detection function per catalogue, no aftershock incompleteness, magnitude errors or mixed magnitude types; real catalogues are harder.

The generating model (Gutenberg-Richter times cumulative-normal detection) is stated in the contract, so a candidate can fit it exactly; the score then measures statistical efficiency on this model rather than robustness to model error.
The generator and its seed are in the evaluator's source; a candidate that re-implements them could reproduce the truth, so results are only meaningful for candidates that use the magnitudes alone.
A better score is a better estimator on this benchmark, not a seismological discovery.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives the generating parameters, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.

tasks.name: Earth science: El Nino-Southern Oscillation forecasts of the Nino 3.4 index
tasks.description: Fit a statistical ENSO forecast model on 1950-1999 ERSSTv5 sea-surface temperatures and, for every month from 2000 to 2024, forecast the monthly Nino 3.4 index for the next 12 months using only data up to that month. The score is the mean root-mean-square error over the 12 lead times.
tasks.contract: fit_enso_model(training) -> model; model.forecast(history) -> float array (12,) of the Nino 3.4 area-mean sea-surface temperature (deg C, ERSSTv5) for each of the 12 months after the last month in history. training and history are dicts of numpy arrays over consecutive months: year, month (1-12), nino12, nino3, nino34 and nino4 (cosine-weighted mean SST, deg C, over grid cells centred in 0-10S 90-80W, 5N-5S 150-90W, 5N-5S 170-120W and 5N-5S 160E-150W) and sst (months, 31, 86): ERSSTv5 SST on its 2-degree grid for 30S-30N (latitude ascending) and 120E-70W (longitude 120 to 290 deg E), NaN over land; training also holds lat (31,) and lon (86,). training covers 1950-01 to 1999-12. Forecasts are then requested in order for every origin month from 2000-01 to 2024-12; history holds all months from 1950-01 up to and including the origin month and nothing later. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 120 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: mean over leads 1-12 of the root-mean-square error (deg C) over the 300 origins; lower is better. Wrong shapes, NaN or values outside [10, 40] deg C are invalid

sources.locator: Ham, Kim and Luo (2019): statistical (deep-learning) ENSO forecasts of the Nino 3.4 index at leads up to 18 months, verified by lead-dependent correlation skill against observed SST.
Barnston et al. (2012): skill of real-time dynamical and statistical Nino 3.4 predictions during 2002-2011, the operational context for statistical ENSO forecasting.
Huang et al. (2017): ERSSTv5, the 2-degree monthly SST reconstruction whose tropical Pacific values and Nino-box means the task uses.
NOAA ERSSTv5 monthly means distributed by NOAA PSL (retrieved 2026-11-20; no constraints on use); months 1950-01 to 2025-12 are used.

limitations: Inputs are sea-surface temperatures only (Nino indices and the 2-degree tropical Pacific field); operational forecasts also use subsurface ocean heat content, winds and coupled dynamical models, so scores are not comparable with published operational skill.

The Nino indices are computed locally as cosine-weighted means over ERSSTv5 cells centred in each box; they reproduce the familiar NOAA ONI peaks to about 0.1 deg C (checked for 1982/83, 1997/98, 2015/16 and 2023/24) but are not the official index files.

The 300 monthly origins are strongly autocorrelated (about 25 independent years and only a handful of strong events), so score differences of a few hundredths of a degree are not statistically meaningful.

ERSSTv5 is recomputed monthly by NOAA and every update revises recent years (NCEI rewrites its monthly files from January 2008 on; the update of November 2026 changed tropical Pacific cells in 52 months from December 2017, mostly one or two cells by 0.01 deg C, and left the Nino 3.4 series unchanged). The derived-file hash check then fails, so preparation needs an archived copy of the locked source file or a re-recorded lock, which changes inputs slightly.
A better score is a better statistical forecast model on these years, not a scientific discovery; the held-out observations are public, so search feedback on this fixed split can overfit it.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives verifying months, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.

tasks.name: Earth science: probabilistic aftershock forecasts after large earthquakes worldwide
tasks.description: Fit an aftershock forecasting model on 1990-2014 sequences from the global ComCat catalogue and, for every large shallow earthquake of 2015-2024, forecast the probability distribution of the number of magnitude 5 or larger aftershocks in the week after day 1 and the month after day 7, using only events before each forecast. The score is the mean logarithmic score of the observed counts.
tasks.contract: fit_aftershock_model(history, training_cases, info) -> model; model.forecast(history, case) -> float array (17,) of probabilities (each >= 1e-9, summing to 1 within 1e-6) that the number of target earthquakes falls in the bins [0], [1], ..., [9], [10-14], [15-19], [20-29], [30-49], [50-99], [100-199], [200 or more] (info['bin_edges'] = 0, 1, ..., 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 100, 200). history is a dict of numpy arrays t (days since 1980-01-01 00:00 UTC), lat, lon, depth (km) and mag of all ComCat earthquakes with magnitude >= 5 worldwide, sorted by time. A case is a dict of floats main_t, main_lat, main_lon, main_depth, main_mag (a shallow, depth <= 70 km, magnitude >= 6 mainshock that is not within the zone of an equal or larger event of the previous 365 days), start (main_t + 1 or main_t + 7 days), window_days (7 or 30) and radius_km = max(50, 2 * 10^(0.5 main_mag - 1.8)); the target is the number of magnitude >= 5 events at any depth within radius_km of the mainshock epicentre during [start, start + window_days). training_cases holds the same fields plus the observed count for the 4207 cases with start before 2015-01-01, and the fit-time history holds the events before 2015-01-01. Forecasts are then requested in order of start for the 1443 cases starting from 2015-01-01 to 2024-11-22; history then holds every event before the case's start and nothing later. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 240 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: mean natural-log probability assigned to the observed bins; higher is better. Wrong shapes, NaN, probabilities below 1e-9 or not summing to 1 are invalid

sources.locator: Reasenberg and Jones (1989): aftershock probabilities from the Gutenberg-Richter and modified Omori laws (the model family of the seed and the reference).
Page et al. (2016): global aftershock forecasts with regional parameters, early-catalogue incompleteness and negative-binomial inter-sequence variability.
USGS ANSS Comprehensive Catalog (ComCat, doi:10.5066/F7MS3QZH): earthquakes of magnitude >= 5 worldwide, 1980-2024 (public domain; retrieved 2026-10-10).

limitations: Mainshock selection (magnitude >= 6, depth <= 70 km, not inside the zone of an equal or larger event of the previous year) and the aftershock radius max(50, 2 * 10^(0.5 M - 1.8)) km are simple local rules, not the regionalised zones of operational forecasts; events of other sequences inside the radius are counted.

Global ComCat magnitudes mix types (mb, Ms, Mw) and the catalogue is incomplete in the first hours and days after large mainshocks, so counts of magnitude >= 5 events are those of the catalogue as distributed.
Counts are scored in 17 bins with the logarithmic score; probabilities below 1e-9 are not allowed, so one confident miss costs at most about 21 nats.
Forecasts of the two windows of one mainshock and of overlapping sequences are not independent; the 1443 test forecasts come from 723 mainshocks.
ComCat is a live catalogue; if past events are revised, the derived-file hash check fails and the data must be re-recorded, which changes scores slightly.

A better score is a better statistical aftershock forecasting model on these years, not a scientific discovery; the held-out catalogue is public, so search feedback on this fixed split can overfit it.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives events after a forecast start, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.

Three training cases start in the last days of 2014 and their target windows end after 2015-01-01 (all three counts are zero), so the fit-time counts reflect up to 18 days of the test period; one of them overlaps by one day the 30-day test window of the same mainshock.

tasks.description: Fit a model of annual global mean surface temperature on the 1850-1979 HadCRUT5 record, given radiative forcing histories and an ENSO index for 1750-2024, and predict the 1980-2024 anomalies without seeing any later temperature. The score is the root-mean-square error of the predicted anomalies.
tasks.contract: predict_gmst(training, inputs) -> float array (45,) of annual global mean near-surface temperature anomalies (deg C from 1961-1990, HadCRUT5 analysis) for 1980-2024. training holds year (1850-1979), gmst and its 95% range gmst_low, gmst_high. inputs holds forcing_year (1750-2024) and forcing, a dict of annual effective radiative forcing series (W m-2, Forster et al. 2025 update of IPCC AR6) for CO2, CH4, N2O, halogen, minor, O3, H2O_stratospheric, contrails, aerosol-radiation_interactions, aerosol-cloud_interactions, BC_on_snow, land_use, solar, volcanic, anthro and total; enso_year, enso_month and relative_nino34 (1854-01 to 2024-12: ERSSTv5 Nino 3.4 anomaly minus the 20S-20N mean SST anomaly, from 1951-1980 monthly climatologies); and predict_years (1980-2024). No temperature after 1979 is provided. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 60 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: root-mean-square error (deg C) of the 45 predicted anomalies against HadCRUT5; lower is better. Wrong shapes, NaN or values outside [-5, 5] deg C are invalid

sources.locator: Lean and Rind (2008): multiple regression of observed global and regional temperature on anthropogenic, volcanic, solar and ENSO influences.
Haustein et al. (2017): a simple impulse-response climate model fitted to observed temperature and forcing to attribute warming (Global Warming Index).
Otto et al. (2013): energy-budget estimates of transient and equilibrium climate response from observed warming and forcing.
Morice et al. (2021): HadCRUT5, the global temperature analysis whose annual means and 95% ranges are the target.
Forster et al. (2025): Indicators of Global Climate Change 2024, the effective radiative forcing time series 1750-2024 used as inputs.
HadCRUT5.0.2.0 global annual summary series (Open Government Licence; retrieved 2026-10-10); 1850-2024 used.
Best-estimate ERF aggregates 1750-2024 (output/ERF_best_aggregates_1750-2024.csv, MIT licence) at a pinned commit.

limitations: The forcing inputs are not independent of the target: the assessed aerosol forcing behind the AR6 and 2024 updates uses observational constraints that include the recent warming, so the held-out period leaks partly into the inputs.

Recent global temperatures are widely known; a candidate can encode remembered values or trends instead of inferring them from 1850-1979, so the score measures emulation skill only for candidates restricted to the training data. Freeze a candidate and test it on later years before any claim.

Only 45 annual values are scored and internal variability not explained by the ENSO index (roughly 0.1 deg C per year) limits the attainable error; HadCRUT5 itself has a 95% range of about 0.03-0.05 deg C in this period.
A better score is a better statistical or physical emulator of observed warming given these forcings, not by itself a new estimate of climate sensitivity.
HadCRUT5 is a live product; if past annual means are revised, the derived-file hash check fails and the data must be re-recorded.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives temperatures after 1979, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.

tasks.name: Earth science: Great Lakes wave height from buoy meteorology
tasks.description: Learn how wind and other meteorology at seven NOAA buoys on Lakes Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie generate waves from 2009-2018 records, then hindcast the hourly significant wave height for 2019-2024 from the buoys' meteorology alone. The score is the root-mean-square error of the hindcast wave heights.
tasks.contract: hindcast_waves(train, test) -> dict {buoy: float array (n_targets,)} of significant wave height (m, 0 to 20) at the target hours of each buoy. train and test map the NDBC buoys 45001, 45006 (Lake Superior), 45002, 45007 (Lake Michigan), 45003, 45008 (Lake Huron) and 45005 (Lake Erie) to dicts with lat, lon, hour (hours since 2009-01-01 00 UTC, one value per observed hour, ascending) and hourly arrays wdir (deg true, direction the wind comes from), wspd and gst (m/s, at the buoy's anemometer height), pres (hPa), atmp, wtmp and dewp (deg C), NaN when missing (for each field the valid value closest to the full hour). train covers 2009-2018 and also holds the wave fields wvht (significant wave height, m), dpd and apd (dominant and average period, s) and mwd (deg); test covers 2019-2024 without wave fields and holds target_index (float indices into hour where a wave height was observed). Meteorology at any test hour, earlier or later, may be used. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 180 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: root-mean-square error (m) over all 177719 target hours; lower is better. Missing buoys, wrong shapes, NaN or values outside [0, 20] m are invalid

sources.locator: Schwab et al. (1984): a simple parametric numerical wave prediction model for Lake Erie driven by observed winds and verified against wave measurements.
Kahma and Calkoen (1992): fetch-limited growth laws of wind-generated waves, the physics behind fetch- and duration-limited wave models.
Donelan, Hamilton and Hui (1985): wave growth and spectra measured in Lake Ontario.
NOAA NDBC historical standard meteorological files of buoys 45001, 45002, 45003, 45005, 45006, 45007 and 45008, 2009-2024 (public domain; retrieved 2026-10-10).

limitations: Only point meteorology at the buoys is available, not the wind field over the lake, so fetch and duration effects must be inferred statistically; operational wave models use gridded winds and are not comparable.
Buoys are deployed only in the ice-free season and the hindcast uses each buoy's own record, so the score covers open-water months at these seven locations only.
Since 2019 the archive holds 10-minute records; the evaluator keeps, for every field, the valid value closest to each full hour, so some hourly values come from up to 30 minutes away.
A better score is a better statistical or physical wave hindcast at these buoys, not a scientific discovery; the held-out observations are public, so search feedback on this split can overfit it.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives 2019-2024 wave observations, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.

tasks.name: Earth science: Atlantic hurricane intensity forecasting from the best track
tasks.description: Fit a statistical tropical-cyclone intensity model on the 1950-2014 Atlantic best track and forecast the 12-120 h maximum sustained wind for every advisory-time record of the held-out 2015-2024 storms. The score is the mean absolute intensity error over seven lead times.
tasks.contract: fit_intensity_model(training_storms) -> model; model.forecast(history) -> float array (7,) of forecast maximum sustained 1-min 10-m winds (kt) at 12, 24, 36, 48, 72, 96 and 120 h. Storms are dicts with numpy arrays time_hours (hours since 1950-01-01 00 UTC), month, day, hour, day_of_year, lat (deg N), lon (deg E, west negative), vmax_kt, mslp_hpa (NaN when missing), plus year (int) and status (list of HURDAT2 codes TD, TS, HU, EX, SD, SS, LO, WV, DB), one entry per 6-hourly synoptic record. training_storms are the 1950-2014 Atlantic HURDAT2 storms. Forecasts are requested in chronological order for every 6-hourly record of a held-out 2015-2024 storm at which it is TD/TS/HU/SD/SS and that verifies at one or more leads; history holds that storm's records up to and including the forecast time and nothing later. A lead verifies only if the storm is still TD/TS/HU/SD/SS at the verifying time (NHC convention). The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 120 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: mean over the seven leads of the mean absolute error (kt) against the best-track maximum wind; lower is better. Values outside [0, 300] kt, NaN or wrong shapes are invalid

sources.locator: Knaff et al. (2003): SHIFOR5, five-day statistical intensity forecasts from climatology and persistence.
Landsea and Franklin (2013): HURDAT2 format, content and best-track uncertainty.
HURDAT2 Atlantic best track, release of 4 April 2025 (1851-2024); public domain; the 1950-2024 synoptic records are used.
NHC 2024 forecast verification report: Tables 2 and 4 give 2019-2023 mean official, CLIPER5 and Decay-SHIFOR5 errors by lead.

limitations: Only best-track history is available (no sea-surface temperature, wind shear, land mask or forecast track), so rapid intensification and landfall decay can be anticipated only from history, date and position; official forecasts use far more information.
Best-track maximum winds are rounded to 5 kt and carry analysis uncertainty of roughly 10 kt or more for weaker systems (Landsea and Franklin 2013), which bounds achievable errors.
A better score is a better statistical intensity model on these seasons, not a scientific discovery.
The held-out observations are public, so search feedback on this fixed split can overfit it; freeze a candidate and test it on later or independent data before claiming a scientific improvement.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that receives a storm's best track only up to the forecast time, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.

tasks.name: Earth science: Atlantic hurricane wind-radii (storm size) forecasting
tasks.description: Fit a model of tropical-cyclone size on the 2004-2014 Atlantic best track and forecast the radius of 34-kt winds in four quadrants 12-72 h ahead for every analysed time of the 2015-2024 storms, given the storm's history and its best-track track and intensity at the verifying times. The score is the mean absolute radius error.
tasks.contract: fit_radii_model(training_storms) -> model; model.forecast(history, future) -> float array (5, 4) of 34-kt wind radii (n mi) in the NE, SE, SW and NW quadrants at 12, 24, 36, 48 and 72 h. training_storms is a list of the 2004-2014 Atlantic HURDAT2 storms as dicts with numpy arrays time_hours (hours since 2004-01-01 00 UTC), lat (deg N), lon (deg E, west negative), vmax_kt, mslp_hpa (NaN when missing) and r34, r50, r64 ((n, 4) radii in n mi for NE, SE, SW, NW; 0 where the threshold is not reached in a quadrant, NaN when not analysed), plus status (list of HURDAT2 codes) and year, one entry per 6-hourly synoptic record. Forecasts are requested in chronological order from every 6-hourly record of a 2015-2024 storm that is TS, HU or SS with maximum wind >= 34 kt and analysed 34-kt radii and that verifies at one or more leads; history holds that storm's records up to and including the forecast time (same fields); future holds lead_hours, verifies (1 or 0) and the best-track lat, lon, vmax_kt and mslp_hpa at each lead (NaN where the lead does not verify). A lead verifies when the storm is then TS, HU or SS with maximum wind >= 34 kt and analysed 34-kt radii. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 120 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: mean over the five leads of the mean absolute error (n mi) over verifying cases and the four quadrants; lower is better. Wrong shapes, NaN or values outside [0, 1000] n mi are invalid

sources.locator: Knaff, Sampson and DeMaria (2007): climatology-and-persistence prediction of tropical-cyclone wind radii driven by the track and intensity forecast.
Knaff et al. (2017): a global statistical-dynamical wind-radii forecast scheme.
Landsea and Franklin (2013): HURDAT2 format, including the four-quadrant wind radii since 2004, and their analysis uncertainty.
HURDAT2 Atlantic best track, release of 4 April 2025 (public domain); the 2004-2024 synoptic records with wind radii are used.

limitations: Best-track wind radii are post-season analyses with large uncertainty (often tens of percent for the 34-kt radii), which bounds the attainable error.

The verifying track, maximum wind and pressure are given (perfect prognosis); operational radii forecasts must use forecast track and intensity, so errors here are smaller than operational ones and not comparable with them.
Only 34-kt radii are scored, at 6-hourly synoptic times; 50- and 64-kt radii and the radius of maximum wind are available as history but not forecast.
A better score is a better statistical storm-size model on these seasons, not a scientific discovery; the held-out observations are public, so search feedback on this split can overfit it.

tasks.name: Earth science: monthly Mauna Loa CO2 forecasts
tasks.description: Fit a forecast model of atmospheric CO2 on the Mauna Loa monthly record up to 1999, together with an ENSO index, and for every month from 2000 to 2024 forecast the next 12 monthly means using only data up to that month. The score is the mean root-mean-square error over the 12 lead times.
tasks.contract: fit_co2_model(training) -> model; model.forecast(history) -> float array (12,) of monthly mean atmospheric CO2 at Mauna Loa (ppm, NOAA GML/SIO record) for each of the 12 months after the last month in history. training and history are dicts of numpy arrays over consecutive months from 1958-03: year, month, co2_ppm, measured_days (number of measurement days; -1 for interpolated months and for the 1958-1974 Scripps values) and relative_nino34 (ERSSTv5 Nino 3.4 anomaly minus the 20S-20N mean SST anomaly, from 1951-1980 monthly climatologies). training ends in 1999-12. Forecasts are then requested in order for every origin month from 2000-01 to 2024-12; history holds all months up to and including the origin month and nothing later. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 120 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: mean over leads 1-12 of the root-mean-square error (ppm) over the 300 origins, using only measured (not interpolated) verifying months; lower is better. Wrong shapes, NaN or values outside [250, 600] ppm are invalid

sources.locator: Betts et al. (2016): forecasting the annual rise of Mauna Loa CO2 from emissions and ENSO (the record 2015/16 rise).
Betts et al. (2018): verification of that operational CO2-rise forecast.
NOAA GML monthly mean CO2 at Mauna Loa (Scripps data before May 1974), March 1958 to December 2025; retrieved 2026-10-10; freely available under the GML data-use statement.
NOAA ERSSTv5 monthly SST used for the relative Nino 3.4 input (no constraints on use).

limitations: Only the CO2 record and an ENSO index are given; operational forecasts also use fossil-fuel emission estimates, so scores are not comparable with them.

Monthly means carry weather-driven noise of a few tenths of a ppm, and December 2022 - July 2023 values come from Maunakea after the Mauna Loa eruption; differences of a few hundredths of a ppm between candidates are not meaningful.
The 300 origins overlap strongly, so the effective sample is about 25 annual growth anomalies.

The GML file is rewritten monthly and old values are revised (ten monthly means of 1974-2014 changed by 0.01 ppm between the files of October and November 2026), so preparation uses the Internet Archive capture of the retrieved file that the data lock names. The ENSO index comes from the live ERSSTv5 file; if its values up to 2024 are revised, the derived-file hash check fails and the data must be re-recorded.
A better score is a better statistical forecast on these years, not a scientific discovery; the record is public, so search feedback can overfit it.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives months after a forecast origin, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.

tasks.name: Earth science: river nitrate loads from sparse samples
tasks.description: Estimate daily nitrate concentrations in eight U.S. rivers from about 16 samples per year and continuous daily discharge, as in routine water-quality monitoring. The score is the error of the resulting monthly nitrate loads against loads computed from continuous in-situ nitrate sensors, which the candidate never sees.
tasks.contract: estimate_nitrate(sites) -> dict {site_number: float array (n_days,)} of daily mean nitrate plus nitrite concentrations (mg/L as N, 0 to 100) for every day of each site's record. sites maps eight USGS site numbers to dicts with day (days since 1970-01-01, ascending, gaps where discharge is missing), decimal_year, discharge_m3s (daily mean discharge, m3/s, every day), sample_index (float indices into day of the sampled days: one random sensor day per calendar month plus four random days per water year with discharge in the site's top 20 percent), sample_nitrate_mg_l (the sensor daily means on those days), lat, lon and drainage_area_km2. Sensor concentrations on other days are never provided. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 120 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: mean over site-months (calendar months with at least 25 approved sensor days, 959 in all) of the absolute relative error (percent) of the monthly load sum(C * Q) over the sensor days, using the predicted instead of the sensor concentrations; lower is better. Missing sites, wrong shapes, NaN or values outside [0, 100] mg/L are invalid

sources.locator: Hirsch, Moyer and Archfield (2010): weighted regressions on time, discharge and season (WRTDS) for river concentrations and fluxes from sparse samples; the evaluator's reference implements its weighting (half-windows 7 years, 2 log units, half a year; at least 100 samples).
Lee et al. (2016): evaluation of stream-load estimation methods against loads from densely sampled records.
Pellerin et al. (2016): continuous in-situ nitrate sensor networks of the USGS, the source of the daily verification data.

USGS NWIS daily values of discharge (00060) and nitrate plus nitrite (99133) for eight sites, 2008 to water year 2025 (public domain; retrieved 2026-10-10); only approved, non-estimated sensor values are used as truth.

limitations: The samples are drawn from the sensor record by a fixed random design rather than being real laboratory analyses, so they carry sensor rather than laboratory error and no sampling-time bias; real monitoring programmes differ.
Loads are computed only over days with approved sensor data in months with at least 25 such days, so winter gaps (sensors removed for ice) and storms missed by the sensors are not scored.
Sites are large Midwest and lower-Mississippi rivers with strong agricultural nitrate signals; the score says little about small streams or other regions.

NWIS daily values are live and provisional values are approved long after the measurements; each record therefore ends where its approved discharge ended when the lock was recorded on 2026-10-10 (2024-04-14 at Baton Rouge, 2025-09-30 at the other sites). If approved values are revised, the derived-file hash check fails and the data must be re-recorded.

The WRTDS reference is a local implementation following the published method (no edge adjustment); it was checked to recover an exact log-linear model but was not compared with the EGRET package, whose geospatial dependencies were not installed.
A better score is a better load-estimation method on these records, not a scientific discovery; the sensor data are public, so search feedback can overfit them.

tasks.contract: forecast_ice(history, past_climate_covariates, lead_months) -> (448,304) probabilities in[0,1] for monthly concentration>=0.15. Six actual NOAA/NSIDC G02202 v02r00 forecasts: July-December2013/2014 monthly histories predict next-year January/March/June at1/3/6-month leads. Native25km grid; area-weighted Brier over valid ocean north of60N using ellipsoidal cell areas, projected-km symmetric edge-distance diagnostic. Land/coast/pole-hole/missing flags excluded. Zeros outside supplied history_ocean_mask are placeholders. No future fields cross API. Historical NOAA observational adaptation, not original IceNet OSISAF data or leaderboard reproduction.

tasks.name: Earth science: snow water equivalent from snow depth at unseen stations
tasks.description: Convert daily snow depth to snow water equivalent at 48 held-out SNOTEL stations across the western United States and Alaska, after learning from 114 other stations with both measurements over water years 2006-2025. The score is the root-mean-square error of snow water equivalent on the held-out stations' snow days.
tasks.contract: estimate_swe(train, test) -> dict {station_triplet: float array (n_targets,)} of snow water equivalent (mm, 0 to 10000) on the held-out target days of each test station. train and test map SNOTEL station triplets to dicts with state, lat, lon, elevation_m, precip_normal_mm (median water-year precipitation 2006-2015), day (days since 1970-01-01 of every day with a valid or edited snow-depth value, water years 2006-2025), depth_cm (snow depth on those days) and target_index (float indices into day of the scored days: depth >= 10.16 cm, SWE >= 10.16 mm, bulk density 0.05-0.65, both values flagged valid); train stations (114) also hold swe_mm (snow-pillow SWE on every day, NaN when not valid), test stations (48, 30 percent of each state) do not. Depth on all days, including later ones, may be used. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 180 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: root-mean-square error (mm) over the 103150 held-out target days; lower is better. Missing stations, wrong shapes, NaN or values outside [0, 10000] mm are invalid

sources.locator: Sturm et al. (2010): estimating snow water equivalent from snow depth with a density model in depth and day of year by snow class; the evaluator's reference uses this functional form with coefficients fitted on the training stations.
Hill et al. (2019): converting snow depth to snow water equivalent using climatological variables, evaluated on independent stations.
USDA NRCS Air and Water Database REST API: SNOTEL daily SNWD, WTEQ and PREC for 162 stations, water years 2006-2025 (public domain; retrieved 2026-10-10).

limitations: Snow-pillow SWE and ultrasonic depth are point measurements with their own errors (pillow bridging, depth sensor noise, depth reported in whole inches); only values flagged valid are scored and implausible densities (outside 0.05-0.65) are excluded.

The hold-out is spatial (unseen stations) but the training stations cover the same years and weather, so performance in other years or at non-SNOTEL sites (lower elevations, shallow snow, forest openings) may differ.
Only station metadata and a precipitation normal are given as climate information; gridded climatologies used by published models are not, so scores are not comparable with them.

The Sturm-form reference is fitted on the training stations (its maximum-density parameter ends at the upper bound 1.0, so the fitted curve is nearly linear); published coefficients were not used because the paper could not be retrieved here.
SNOTEL data are revised by NRCS; if values change, the derived-file hash check fails and the data must be re-recorded.
A better score is a better depth-to-SWE conversion on this network, not a scientific discovery; the data are public, so search feedback can overfit them.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives the held-out stations' SWE, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.
provenance.benchmark: Earth science: snow water equivalent from snow depth at unseen stations
