tasks.name: Earth science: one-day earthquake forecasts for southern California
tasks.description: Fit an earthquake occurrence model on the 1981-2015 southern California ComCat catalogue and, for every day of 2016-2024, forecast the expected number of magnitude 3.45 or larger earthquakes in each 0.1-degree cell using only events before that day. The score is the information gain per earthquake of the Poisson likelihood over a time-independent smoothed-seismicity reference.
tasks.contract: fit_quake_model(training, grid) -> model; model.forecast(history, day) -> float array (50, 70) of the expected number of target earthquakes (magnitude >= 3.45, depth <= 30 km) during [day, day + 1) in each 0.1-degree cell: row i is latitude 32.0 + 0.1 i to 32.1 + 0.1 i deg N, column j is longitude -121.0 + 0.1 j to -120.9 + 0.1 j deg E (grid['lat_edges'] (51,), grid['lon_edges'] (71,)). training and history are dicts of numpy arrays t (days since 1981-01-01 00:00 UTC), lat, lon (deg), depth (km) and mag of all ComCat earthquakes with magnitude >= 2.5 in 31-38 N, 122-113 W, sorted by time; training holds the events before 2016-01-01. grid also gives target_min_magnitude 3.45, target_max_depth_km 30, first_forecast_day 12783 (2016-01-01) and last_forecast_day 16070 (2024-12-31). Forecasts are requested in order for every day from 2016-01-01 to 2024-12-31 (day is the float day number); history then holds every event before 00:00 UTC of that day and nothing later. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 300 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: information gain per target earthquake (nats) of the joint Poisson log-likelihood of the observed daily cell counts (1047 target events) over the evaluator's time-independent reference (1981-2015 epicentres smoothed with a 0.15-degree Gaussian kernel and scaled to the 1981-2015 target rate); higher is better. Rates below 1e-10, NaN, wrong shapes or daily totals above 1e4 are invalid

sources.locator: Helmstetter, Kagan and Jackson (2006): one-day forecasts of southern California earthquakes on a 0.1-degree grid, comparing short-term (clustering) and time-independent models by likelihood.
Ogata (1988): the epidemic-type aftershock sequence (ETAS) point-process model of earthquake occurrence.
Zechar, Gerstenberger and Rhoades (2010): Poisson joint-likelihood tests of gridded earthquake forecasts used by CSEP; the task uses the joint log-likelihood and reports the N-test ratio.
USGS ANSS Comprehensive Catalog (ComCat, doi:10.5066/F7MS3QZH), FDSN event service: earthquakes with magnitude >= 2.5 in 31-38 N, 122-113 W, 1981-2024 (public domain; retrieved 2026-11-20).

limitations: The test region is a 0.1-degree rectangle (32-37 N, 121-114 W) rather than the CSEP southern California polygon; it includes offshore and northern Baja California cells where the catalogue is less complete.

ComCat mixes magnitude types (mostly local and moment magnitudes) and is incomplete in the hours after large mainshocks; targets are the catalogue as distributed, not a homogenised or declustered catalogue.
Forecasts are issued once per day at 00:00 UTC and verified on daily cell counts; magnitudes and depths of target events are not scored (no magnitude or depth test).

The 2016-2024 period is dominated by the 2019 Ridgecrest sequence, so the score mostly reflects aftershock forecasting skill for one large sequence; the information gain is an estimate with substantial sampling uncertainty.
ComCat is a live catalogue; if past events are revised, the derived-file hash check fails and the data must be re-recorded, which changes scores slightly.
A better score is a better statistical forecast model on these years, not a scientific discovery; the held-out catalogue is public, so search feedback on this fixed split can overfit it.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives events after a forecast day starts, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.
provenance.benchmark: Earth science: one-day earthquake forecasts for southern California
provenance.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

tasks.name: Earth science: diffuse solar irradiance from global irradiance at unseen stations
tasks.description: Learn a separation model from 1-minute measurements of global, direct and diffuse solar irradiance at four NOAA SURFRAD stations and estimate the diffuse irradiance at three other stations from their global irradiance, solar geometry and meteorology on 48 days of 2022-2023. The score is the root-mean-square error of the estimated diffuse irradiance.
tasks.contract: estimate_diffuse(train, test) -> dict {station: float array (n_targets,)} of 1-minute diffuse horizontal irradiance (W m-2, 0 to 1500) at the target minutes of each test station. train (Bondville, Desert Rock, Fort Peck, Goodwin Creek: bon, dra, fpk, gwn) and test (Penn State, Sioux Falls, Table Mountain: psu, sxf, tbl) map station codes to dicts with lat, lon, elevation_m and arrays over every daytime minute (solar zenith < 90 deg) of days 8, 23, ..., 353 of 2022 and 2023: day (days since 2022-01-01), minute (UTC minute of day), zen (solar zenith angle, deg), ghi (global horizontal irradiance), e0_horizontal (1361 (1 + 0.033 cos(2 pi doy/365)) cos(zen)), temp (deg C), rh (%), pres (hPa), NaN where SURFRAD's quality flag is not 0, and target_index (float indices of the scored minutes). train also holds dni (direct normal) and dhi (diffuse) irradiance; test does not. Measurements at any minute of a test day may be used. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 180 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: root-mean-square error (W m-2) over the 87316 test-station target minutes (zenith < 85 deg, GHI >= 10 W m-2, all three components flagged good and closing within max(20 W m-2, 8 percent of GHI)); lower is better. Missing stations, wrong shapes, NaN or values outside [0, 1500] are invalid

sources.locator: Erbs, Klein and Duffie (1982): diffuse fraction as a function of the clearness index, the classic separation model.
Ridley, Boland and Lauret (2010): logistic separation model with multiple predictors (the seed is its single-predictor form).
Yang (2022): review and worldwide comparison of 1-minute separation models, the evaluation setting followed here.
Augustine et al. (2000): the SURFRAD network and its measurements.
SURFRAD 1-minute daily files of seven stations, 48 days of 2022-2023 (public domain; retrieved 2026-10-11).

limitations: Only 48 sampled days per station (every 15th day of 2022 and 2023) are used, and the three test stations are mid-latitude continental U.S. sites; separation models behave differently in other climates.

The truth is the measured diffuse irradiance after quality control (flags, closure within 8 percent or 20 W m-2); measurement uncertainty of a few percent remains, and rejected minutes (often broken clouds or instrument issues) are not scored.
No clear-sky irradiance model or aerosol data are given; candidates must build any clear-sky reference themselves from the inputs.
A better score is a better separation model for these stations, not a scientific discovery; the data are public, so search feedback can overfit them.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives the test stations' direct or diffuse irradiance, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.

tasks.name: Earth science: species distribution models from presence-only records
tasks.description: Fit species distribution models for 226 anonymised species in six regions from presence-only records, background points and environmental covariates, and score sites of independent presence-absence surveys whose outcomes are withheld. The score is the mean area under the ROC curve over species.
tasks.contract: predict_distributions(regions) -> dict {region: {species_id: float array (n_sites,)}} of habitat-suitability scores (any finite real numbers; only their ranking matters) at the presence-absence survey sites of each species' biological group. regions maps AWT, CAN, NSW, NZ, SA and SWI to dicts with covariates (list of k names), categorical (names of categorical covariates: CAN ontveg, NSW vegsys, NZ age and toxicats, SWI calc), coordinates (text naming the x/y system), presence {species_id: {'x': (n, k) covariate values, 'xy': (n, 2) coordinates}} of presence-only records, background {'x': (m, k), 'xy': (m, 2)} of random background points, and sites {group: {'x': (s, k), 'xy': (s, 2), 'species': [ids of the species evaluated at these sites]}}; NaN marks a missing covariate value. Presence-absence outcomes at the sites are never provided. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 300 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: mean over the 226 species of the area under the ROC curve (tied scores count one half) of the site scores against the observed presences and absences; higher is better. Missing species, wrong shapes or non-finite scores are invalid

sources.locator: Elith et al. (2006): comparison of species distribution modelling methods fitted to presence-only data and evaluated with independent presence-absence data in the same six regions.
Elith et al. (2020): description of the released benchmark data (226 species, presence-only training, background, presence-absence evaluation).
Valavi et al. (2022): benchmark of presence-only methods on these data with AUC as the main evaluation measure.
OSF project SDM_NCEAS (CC BY 4.0): train_po, train_bg, test_env and test_pa CSV files of the six regions; downloaded files match the SHA-256 hashes published by OSF.

limitations: AUC measures how well site scores rank surveyed presences above absences; it ignores calibration and prevalence, and survey absences include non-detections.
Site and record coordinates are provided, so spatial predictors are allowed; published comparisons mostly used environmental covariates only, so scores are not directly comparable with them.
No published value is embedded: the benchmark paper's tables could not be retrieved in this environment (the publisher's site refused the request), so the mean AUCs it reports were not checked.
The presence-absence outcomes are public on OSF; the sandbox keeps them away from the candidate process, but search feedback on these fixed sites can still overfit them.
A better score is a better species distribution modelling method on this benchmark, not an ecological discovery.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives the survey outcomes, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.

tasks.name: Earth science: homogenisation of monthly temperature networks
tasks.description: Remove non-climatic breaks, drifts and outliers from 40 synthetic networks of ten correlated 100-year monthly temperature records, as climate-data centres do before estimating trends. The score is the mean centred root-mean-square difference between the homogenised and the true annual means, which the generator knows exactly.
tasks.contract: homogenize(networks, calendar) -> list of 40 float arrays (10, 1200): homogenised monthly temperatures (deg C) of each network's stations. networks is a list of 40 arrays (10 stations, 1200 months) of observed monthly mean temperatures (deg C, NaN where missing) of 100-year synthetic networks; calendar holds year (1901-2000) and month (1-12) arrays (1200,). The observations contain non-climatic breaks (about five per century per station, sizes of standard deviation 0.8 deg C with a seasonal cycle; the most recent segment is unbiased), occasional network-wide clustered breaks, gradual drifts, outliers (1 percent, 3-5 deg C) and gaps (late starts, 2 percent random). Returned values at missing months are ignored. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 120 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. Score: mean over the 400 stations of the centred root-mean-square difference between homogenised and true annual means (years with at least 10 observed months, computed over the observed months); lower is better. A wrong list length or array shape, or non-finite or implausible (|value| >= 100) values at observed months are invalid

sources.locator: Venema et al. (2012): the HOME benchmark of homogenisation algorithms for monthly data (surrogate networks, inserted breaks, outliers, drifts and gaps; centred RMSE of annual means), whose design the generator follows.
Williams, Menne and Thorne (2012): benchmarking pairwise homogenisation of U.S. surface temperatures with synthetic worlds.
Alexandersson (1986): the standard normal homogeneity test used by the seed.

limitations: The networks are synthetic: an AR(1) regional signal with a random trend, AR(1) station noise and simple annual cycles, with inhomogeneities drawn from fixed distributions; real networks have more varied correlation structures, break statistics and metadata.
The generator and its seed are in the evaluator's source; a candidate that re-implements them could reproduce the truth, so results are only meaningful for candidates that use the observations alone.
No station metadata (documented relocations or instrument changes) are given, unlike in practical homogenisation.
A better score is a better homogenisation method on this benchmark, not a statement about real climate records.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives the true series, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.
provenance.benchmark: Earth science: homogenisation of monthly temperature networks
provenance.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

tasks.name: Earth science: two-stream closures for solar radiative transfer
tasks.description: Design the coefficients of a two-stream approximation for sunlight in a scattering and absorbing atmospheric layer as functions of single-scattering albedo, asymmetry parameter and solar zenith angle. The evaluator solves the two-stream equations for 12000 layers and scores the mean reflectance and transmittance error against an accurate 96-stream discrete-ordinate solution.
tasks.contract: two_stream_coefficients(omega, g, mu0) -> (gamma1, gamma2, gamma3, f): four float arrays (n,) for n layers given by float arrays omega (single-scattering albedo, 0.5 to 1, exactly 1 for conservative layers), g (Henyey-Greenstein asymmetry parameter, 0 to 0.95) and mu0 (cosine of the solar zenith angle, 0.05 to 1). For each layer the evaluator delta-scales with the forward fraction f (tau' = (1 - omega f) tau, omega' = omega (1 - f) / (1 - omega f)) and solves exactly the two-stream equations dFup/dtau' = gamma1 Fup - gamma2 Fdown - gamma3 omega' exp(-tau'/mu0) and dFdown/dtau' = gamma2 Fup - gamma1 Fdown + (1 - gamma3) omega' exp(-tau'/mu0) (Meador and Weaver 1980; unit beam irradiance, no diffuse light entering at the top, black surface; omega' is capped at 1 - 1e-10) for the layer's optical depth tau, on which the coefficients cannot depend. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas importable; no file, network or subprocess access; one thread) with 60 s of CPU time for fitting and all predictions together; seed any randomness so that results are deterministic. The function is called once with the 3000 distinct (omega, g, mu0) triples of the design, and the coefficients returned for a triple are used at all four of its optical depths. Score: mean over 12000 fixed layers (3000 random triples, a quarter conservative, each at four optical depths, one drawn log-uniformly from each decade of 0.01-100) of |R - R_ref| + |T - T_ref|, where R is the reflectance, T the total (direct plus diffuse) transmittance and the references come from a 96-stream delta-M discrete-ordinate solution; lower is better. Coefficients must satisfy gamma1 > 0, gamma1 >= |gamma2|, 0 <= gamma3 <= 1 and 0 <= f < 1; NaN or wrong shapes are invalid

sources.locator: Meador and Weaver (1980): unified gamma1-gamma3 formulation of two-stream approximations, the coefficient tables of the Eddington and quadrature schemes, and their accuracy against exact solutions.
Joseph, Wiscombe and Weinman (1976): delta-Eddington approximation with forward fraction f = g^2 (the seed).
King and Harshvardhan (1986): comparative accuracy of two-stream and related approximations against exact reflectance and transmittance over optical depth, albedo, asymmetry and solar angle.
Stamnes et al. (1988): the discrete-ordinate method with delta-M scaling and stable eigen-solution that the reference solver follows.

limitations: Only a single homogeneous layer over a black surface with a Henyey-Greenstein phase function and unit beam irradiance is scored; multilayer atmospheres, surface reflection, real cloud or aerosol phase functions and thermal emission are not.

The 12000 layers come from a fixed random design (seed 20261010; 3000 triples of albedo, asymmetry and sun angle, each at four optical depths); the generator and its seed are in the evaluator's source, so a candidate can rebuild the design, but it gains only the four depths at which each triple is scored. A closure tuned to this design may be less accurate for other distributions of optical depth, albedo, asymmetry or sun angle.

The reference is a numerical solution (48 streams per hemisphere, delta-M), not an analytic one: it changes by about 1e-11 when the stream number is doubled and agreed with an independent Monte Carlo simulation to within its sampling error (about 6e-4) on the checked layers; conservative layers are computed with albedo 1 - 1e-10, and the stored fluxes are rounded to six decimals.

Coefficients may depend on albedo, asymmetry and sun angle but not on optical depth; closures that use extra information (for example tabulated corrections) are allowed, so a better score is a more accurate two-stream approximation, not necessarily a cheaper or more physical one.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives the reference fluxes, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.
provenance.benchmark: Earth science: two-stream closures for solar radiative transfer
provenance.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

tasks.name: Economics: Forecasting US industrial production with FRED-MD
tasks.description: Forecast annualized US industrial-production growth 1, 6 and 12 months ahead from the 126-series FRED-MD panel available at each month-end origin from 1990 to 2023. The evaluator recomputes the targets and scores the root-mean-square error relative to a direct autoregressive benchmark with BIC lag selection.
tasks.contract: forecast_target(history, horizons) -> array of 3 floats: forecasts of the task's target 1, 6 and 12 months after the origin (horizons = [1, 6, 12]). tasks.name: Economics: Kidney exchange clearing with two- and three-way cycles
tasks.description: Choose vertex-disjoint two- and three-way exchange cycles in eight public kidney-exchange pools of 256 and 512 incompatible patient-donor pairs to maximize the number of transplants. tasks.contract: select_exchanges(pool) -> list of cycles; each cycle is a list of 2 or 3 distinct pair indices [v1, ..., vk] such that the donor of v1 is compatible with the patient of v2, ..., and the donor of vk with the patient of v1, and no pair appears in two cycles. pool = {'name': str, 'pairs': n (256 or 512), 'edges': (E, 2) int array of compatible (donor_pair, patient_pair), 0-based, 'max_cycle_length': 3, 'time_limit_seconds': 60.0 (advisory)}. Called once for each of eight PrefLib kidney pools (00036-00000151..154 with 256 pairs, 00036-00000191..194 with 512 pairs, no altruists). Score: total transplants (pairs on the chosen cycles) divided by the total proven optimum, 1945 (maximize; 1 is optimal). The whole evaluation must finish within 600 s. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and the other installed packages are importable, while the evaluator's library, its data files, the network and subprocesses are not accessible; one thread and 3 GB of memory. It receives only the arguments described here, one call at a time: the arguments of a call are sent after the value of the previous call has been received. sources.locator: Roth, Sonmez and Unver (2007): kidney exchange with two- and three-way exchanges among incompatible patient-donor pairs and the gains from three-way cycles.
Abraham, Blum and Sandholm (2007): the clearing problem with a cycle-length cap, its NP-hardness for caps of 3 or more, and exact integer-programming clearing for nationwide pools.
Saidman et al. (2006): the pool generator (blood types, PRA levels, spousal donors) used for the PrefLib instances.
PrefLib dataset 00036 (kidney), pinned commit: pools 00036-00000151..154 (256 pairs) and 00036-00000191..194 (512 pairs), no altruists.

limitations: The pools are synthetic (Saidman et al. generator, donated to PrefLib by John Dickerson), not registry data; PrefLib removed other faulty kidney instances in September 2026 and only pools without altruists are used here.

Every pool's optimum is known, so a score of 1 reproduces the integer-programming solution; the 600 s limit makes the task about fast clearing on the larger pools, and time-limited candidates can depend on hardware.

tasks.name: Economics: Efficient school choice under coarse priorities
tasks.description: Assign students to schools when school priorities have many ties, improving on deferred acceptance with a single tie-breaking lottery (DA-STB) while keeping the matching weakly stable. Valid only if every student gets a school on her list or nothing, capacities hold, and the matching is weakly stable: no student prefers a school that has a free seat or admits someone of strictly lower priority there. Abdulkadiroglu, Pathak and Roth (2009): single versus multiple tie-breaking and the efficiency-strategy-proofness trade-off in the redesigned NYC high-school match.
Manlove, Irving, Iwama, Miyazaki and Morita (2002): optimization over weakly stable matchings with ties is NP-hard in general (motivates the integer-programming reference).

limitations: Markets are synthetic (random homes and schools on a unit square, school quality, distance and taste shocks, nested walk zones and 5% siblings); they mimic coarse NYC-style priorities but are not real application data.

Score: monthly Sharpe ratio of the net out-of-sample excess returns over every month of the task period (maximize); the 1/N rule is recomputed on the same months for comparison. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and the other installed packages are importable, while the evaluator's library, its data files, the network and subprocesses are not accessible; one thread and 3 GB of memory. It receives only the arguments described here, one call at a time: the arguments of a call are sent after the value of the previous call has been received. Arguments and return values travel as numbers, strings, lists, dicts with string keys and numeric numpy arrays, so a tuple arrives as a list

tasks.name: Finance: Daily volatility forecasting for US equity portfolios
tasks.description: Forecast the next day's return variance of the US stock market and 49 industry portfolios, updating the forecasts day by day from 2000 to 2025 after a training period ending in 1999. The evaluator reveals each day's returns only after the forecasts are made and scores the QLIKE loss against squared returns.
tasks.contract: make_forecaster(training_returns, names) -> object with forecast() and update(returns). training_returns is a (7280, 50) float array of daily returns (decimal) from 1971-03-12 to 1999-12-31: column 0 is the CRSP value-weighted market (Mkt-RF + RF), columns 1-49 the value-weighted Fama-French industries; names lists the 50 series. The evaluator then walks through the 6,475 trading days 2000-01-03..2025-09-30: forecast() must return a (50,) array of next-day return variances in [1e-10, 1]; afterwards update(r) receives that day's (50,) returns. Score: mean QLIKE loss log(h) + r^2/h over all days and series (minimize); the RiskMetrics EWMA benchmark (lambda 0.94), the difference and a Diebold-Mariano statistic are reported. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and the other installed packages are importable, while the evaluator's library, its data files, the network and subprocesses are not accessible; one thread and 3 GB of memory. It receives only the arguments described here, one call at a time: the arguments of a call are sent after the value of the previous call has been received. Arguments and return values travel as numbers, strings, lists, dicts with string keys and numeric numpy arrays, so a tuple arrives as a list

sources.locator: Hansen and Lunde (2005): out-of-sample comparison of many volatility models against GARCH(1,1) with several loss functions.
Patton (2011): loss functions, including QLIKE, that rank volatility forecasts consistently when the true variance is replaced by a noisy proxy such as the squared return.
Bollerslev (1986): the GARCH model, the classic benchmark for conditional variance forecasts.
Daily Fama/French factors (market = Mkt-RF + RF) and value-weighted 49 industry portfolio returns, CRSP 202509 files pinned in catalog/finance-data-lock.json.

limitations: Squared daily returns are a noisy proxy for the daily variance; QLIKE ranks forecasts consistently with this proxy but the loss level is not a variance-accuracy measure, and intraday realized variances are not available here.
Forecasts are for close-to-close total returns (no mean adjustment); weekends, holidays and overnight effects are treated like any other trading day.

The evaluation period 2000-2025 is public. A candidate that reads the prepared files or memorizes returns can look ahead; the interface only passes returns up to the previous day. Treat scores as development scores.
One data vintage of CRSP value-weighted portfolio returns is used; the 50 series are strongly correlated, so they do not provide 50 independent comparisons.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives later data, realised outcomes or reference solutions, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.

Called at the 415 month-end origins 1990-01..2024-07; |forecast| <= 30. Score: RMSE of the candidate divided by the RMSE of the random walk (no-change forecast), averaged over the three horizons and the maturities 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 and 10 years (minimize; the random-walk seed scores exactly 1). The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and the other installed packages are importable, while the evaluator's library, its data files, the network and subprocesses are not accessible; one thread and 3 GB of memory. sources.locator: Diebold and Li (2006): dynamic Nelson-Siegel forecasting of the yield curve, recursive out-of-sample forecasts 1, 6 and 12 months ahead, RMSE compared with the random walk.

limitations: GSW yields are smoothed fitted values from a Svensson curve, not observed bond yields; fitting error and smoothing make them easier to forecast than raw yields, and maturities below one year are excluded because GSW caution against them.

The evaluation origins (1990-2024) and the data file are public; tuning on them or reading the prepared file can produce look-ahead. Forecasts at different origins overlap for the 6- and 12-month horizons, so the effective sample is smaller than 415.
One data vintage (archived 2025-08-09) is used as if it were real-time; the live file is revised without notice.
RMSE ratios against the random walk have wide sampling uncertainty; Diebold-Mariano statistics per horizon are reported but a ratio slightly below 1 is weak evidence.

tasks.name: Few edges in 5-uniform hypergraphs without Property B (m(5))
tasks.description: construct() -> {'n': n, 'edges': [[v1, ..., v5], ...]}: distinct 5-element edges on vertices 0..n-1 with 5 <= n <= 26 and at most 200 edges. The hypergraph must have no proper 2-colouring (no colouring of the vertices leaves every edge with both colours), checked exactly by backtracking with unit propagation. Minimize the number of edges. A valid hypergraph with e edges certifies m(5) <= e; the best known construction has 51 edges and every 5-uniform hypergraph with at most 28 edges is 2-colourable.

tasks.name: Flattest plus-minus-one polynomials with 24 coefficients (minimum sup norm)

tasks.name: Small 3-regular graph of girth 16 (cage problem n(3,16))
tasks.description: Construct a 3-regular graph with no cycle shorter than 16 on as few vertices as possible. The smallest known such graph has 936 vertices (Exoo, Goedgebeur, Jooken, Stubbe and Van den Eede, 2026) and the best lower bound is 512.
tasks.contract: construct(k, g) -> (n, edges): the number of vertices n and a list of edges (i, j) on vertices 0..n-1; the evaluator passes this task's degree k and girth g. The graph must be simple (no loops or repeated edges), every vertex must have degree exactly k, and no cycle may be shorter than g (certified exactly with non-backtracking walks from every vertex). n must lie between the Moore bound and max_vertices. Score: n, minimized; it is an upper bound on the cage order n(k, g).

sources.locator: Exoo, Goedgebeur, Jooken, Stubbe and Van den Eede, Electron. J. Combin. 33(3) (2026) P3.48 (arXiv:2511.07247), Table 2: n(3,16) >= 512, previous upper bound 960, new upper bound 936; Figure 4 lists the base graph and the group SmallGroup(117,1) = C13 semidirect C9 of the lift.
Record graph n936_k3_g16.g6 in graph6 format (GPL-3.0).
Exoo and Jajcay, Dynamic cage survey (Electron. J. Combin. DS16): definitions, Moore bound and record tables.

limitations: The evaluator accepts at most 50,000 vertices; the explicit Lazebnik-Ustimenko-Woldar seed has 39366 vertices.
Connectivity is not required; a disconnected graph only has more vertices than its components.

The record construction is public, so a candidate can reproduce the record by embedding it; the score measures the returned object, not the search that produced it, and only a strictly smaller score than the best known value is a new result.

tasks.name: Minimal logarithmic energy of 100 points on the sphere
tasks.description: Place 100 points on the unit sphere to minimize the logarithmic energy, the sum over all pairs of log(1/distance), the energy in Smale's 7th problem. The lowest published energy, -1083.377140539, is the putative global minimum: it is not proven minimal, but random-restart local optimisation reproduces it within seconds, so the task measures whether an optimiser reaches it.
tasks.contract: construct() -> array of shape (N, 3) of nonzero vectors; each is normalised to the unit sphere. Score: the logarithmic energy sum_{i<j} log(1 / |x_i - x_j|) (natural logarithm, chordal distances, pair terms summed with math.fsum); minimize. Points closer than 1e-9, a wrong shape or non-finite values make the candidate invalid.

sources.locator: Rakhmanov, Saff and Zhou (1994), Minimal discrete energy on the sphere: the minimal logarithmic and Riesz energy problems and numerical minima.
Nerattini, Brauchart and Kiessling (2014), supplement table 6.2 (s = 0): putatively minimal standardized pair energy v_0(100) = -0.21886406879576, i.e. E = -1083.377140539.

Amore, Figueroa and Ramos (2025), CC BY 4.0 dataset of local minima of the logarithmic energy; LocalMinima.zip, member 100.zip (39 minima for N = 100), whose lowest minimum reproduces the tabulated value to 2.9e-10.

limitations: The record is the lowest published value we could check: the tables of Nerattini, Brauchart and Kiessling (2014), compiled from Rakhmanov, Saff and Zhou (1995) and Calef (2009), and the 2025 landscape survey of Amore, Figueroa and Ramos. R. Womersley's published point sets could not be accessed when the task was prepared, so a lower value in sources we could not read cannot be excluded.
Points are normalised to the unit sphere before scoring, so only directions matter; the record coordinates are public, so scores measure the returned construction, not the search that produced it.
Candidate Python runs inside the evaluator process and is trusted research code; the evaluator recomputes the score from the returned array but does not sandbox the program.

The reference is easy to reach: L-BFGS on the normalised coordinates from random starting points ties it within the 1e-9 margin in about a second (55 of 129 random starts in 35 s on one core for N = 100), no start went below it, and the 39 local minima published by Amore, Figueroa and Ramos (2025) contain no lower value. The headroom of the task is therefore the gap between the seed and this value; a score below it by more than the margin would be a new record and is not expected.
provenance.benchmark: Minimal logarithmic energy of 100 points on the sphere
provenance.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

tasks.name: Covering the sphere with 130 equal caps
tasks.description: Place 130 points on the unit sphere so that the largest angular distance from any point of the sphere to its nearest chosen point (the covering radius) is as small as possible. The best known covering has radius 11.3153512 degrees: in 2026 Henry Cohn improved the 1994 value of Hardin, Sloane and Smith (11.3165625 degrees). It is not proven optimal.
tasks.contract: construct() -> array of shape (N, 3) of nonzero vectors; each is normalised to the unit sphere. Score: the covering radius in degrees, max over points y of the sphere of the angular distance from y to the nearest configuration point (the largest circumradius of the facets of the convex hull, each facet checked to have an empty cap); minimize. Coincident points, configurations inside a closed hemisphere, numerically inconsistent hulls, a wrong shape or non-finite values make the candidate invalid.

tasks.name: Path decompositions of three fixed connected graphs (Gallai's conjecture)
tasks.description: construct() -> three lists of paths (vertex lists), one per fixed instance graph generated by instance_graph(n, p, seed) for (20,0.3,1), (25,0.3,2), (30,0.25,3) in the verifier. Paths must be simple, use graph edges, be edge-disjoint and cover all edges. Minimize the total number of paths; Gallai's conjecture predicts at most 10+13+15 = 38. The score is the total number of paths over three fixed random connected graphs; staying within 38 is consistent with the conjecture, exceeding it is not evidence against it.

tasks.name: Which small gaps occur between consecutive integers coprime to 29#
tasks.description: construct() -> up to 200 certificates [x, g] with 1 <= x <= 29# = 6469693230 and 2 <= g <= 1000, where x and x + g are coprime to 29# and every integer strictly between them shares a prime factor with 29#. tasks.name: Gaussian-prime paths with small maximum jumps
tasks.description: construct() -> a list of distinct integer coordinate pairs in [-64,64]^2, starting at (1,1), ending with max(abs(x),abs(y))>=50, and containing only Gaussian primes. Minimize the largest squared Euclidean step. Axis primes must be 3 modulo 4; off-axis norms must be prime. The finite path minimizes its largest jump inside a bounded square; it does not establish an infinite path or reproduce the periodic-moat proof. The optimum is 8, found by breadth-first search over all Gaussian primes in the box; this is a rediscovery task.

tasks.name: Few cycle lengths under degree and girth constraints

tasks.contract: construct(instance) -> array of shape (n, 3): Cartesian coordinates of n atoms in reduced units (lattice constant 1). instance = {'potential': 'sutton_chen', 'kind': '12-6' | '9-6' | '10-8', 'n': atoms, 'n_exp', 'm_exp', 'c'}; called once for each of six instances (kind, n) = (12-6, 38), (12-6, 75), (9-6, 59), (9-6, 80), (10-8, 55), (10-8, 79); all calls together within 300 s (enforced) and should use at most 4 threads (not enforced by the evaluator). Score: mean over instances of 100*(E - E_pub)/|E_pub| against the putative global minima tabulated by Doye and Wales (1998) (minimize; 0 matches all six, negative is lower). chem_clusters.relax(positions, 'sutton_chen', kind) and chem_clusters.sutton_chen_energy_gradient(positions, kind) may be called

tasks.name: Odd covering systems with moduli dividing 51975 (fewest uncovered residues)
tasks.description: construct() -> classes [[m, r], ...] with distinct moduli m > 1 dividing 51975 = 3^3 * 5^2 * 7 * 11 (hence odd) and 0 <= r < m. The score is the number of residues modulo 51975 covered by no class (exact). Minimize. The score 0 (a covering system with distinct odd moduli) is impossible for this modulus by the necessary condition of Berger, Felzenbaum and Fraenkel (1986). Every divisor of 51975 above 1 is available once. The minimum is positive: an odd covering with distinct moduli needs prod (p-1)/(p-2) - sum 1/(p-2) > 2 over the primes p dividing the least common multiple (Berger, Felzenbaum and Fraenkel), and for 3, 5, 7, 11 the left side is 86/45. The score measures how close systems with this modulus come to a covering; it cannot decide the odd covering problem. No minimum is documented.

tasks.name: Physics: product-formula design for Heisenberg-chain time evolution
tasks.description: Choose the coefficients of a twelve-stage product formula that approximates the time evolution of a six-site Heisenberg chain split into even and odd bonds. The evaluator builds every factor and the exact propagator and scores the mean spectral-norm error at three evolution times.
tasks.contract: coefficients(stages) -> (a, b), two lists of 12 finite numbers in [-50, 50] with sum(a) = sum(b) = 1 (consistency). The evaluator forms the product formula U(t) = S_12 ... S_2 S_1 with S_k = exp(-i b_k t B) exp(-i a_k t A): stage 1 acts first, and within a stage the A factor acts before the B factor. With sites numbered 0..5 and Pauli matrices X, Y, Z, the Hamiltonian of the six-site open XXZ chain (anisotropy 0.8, field 0.3) is H = sum_{j=0..4} (X_j X_{j+1} + Y_j Y_{j+1} + 0.8 Z_j Z_{j+1}) + 0.3 sum_{j=0..5} Z_j = A + B, where A holds the bonds (0,1), (2,3), (4,5) and the field on sites 0, 2, 4, and B holds the bonds (1,2), (3,4) and the field on sites 1, 3, 5. Score (minimize): mean over t = 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0 of the spectral norm ||U(t) - exp(-i t (A + B))||. coefficients runs in a sandboxed subprocess with a 60 s CPU budget

sources.locator: Childs, Su, Tran, Wiebe and Zhu (2021), Theory of Trotter error with commutator scaling: commutator bounds on the spectral-norm error of product formulas for quantum simulation.
Suzuki (1990), Fractal decomposition of exponential operators: the higher-order product formulas built from symmetric splittings.
Blanes and Moan (2002), Practical symplectic partitioned Runge-Kutta and Runge-Kutta-Nystrom methods: optimized splitting coefficients for a fixed number of stages.

limitations: The error is measured on one six-site chain and three evolution times; coefficients tuned here need not be optimal for other Hamiltonians, system sizes or step sizes.
The fixed stage count fixes the cost per step only in this two-group splitting; circuit depth and hardware costs of a quantum implementation are not modelled.
Errors are computed on the full 64-dimensional Hilbert space by dense linear algebra; this is exact for this size but does not scale to larger chains.
No published value exists for this exact chain, stage count and set of times.

tasks.description: Design a symmetric 32x32-pixel unit cell of air and dielectric (epsilon 12) for a two-dimensional square-lattice photonic crystal that opens the largest gap between the fourth and fifth TM bands. tasks.name: Physics: two-dimensional spin-glass ground states on fixed instances
tasks.description: Find ground states of nine Edwards-Anderson spin glasses on 10x10, 15x15 and 20x20 periodic square lattices with Gaussian couplings. The evaluator recomputes the cut weight of every returned spin configuration and compares it with the exact optimum computed for these instances by branch-and-cut.
tasks.contract: ground_state(instance) -> list of instance['nodes'] spins, each -1 or +1. instance has keys name, nodes, side, dimension and edges (list of [i, j, weight] with integer weights and 0-based node indices) of a 2-dimensional periodic grid of side 10, 15 and 20 with Gaussian couplings. ground_state is called once per instance in a sandboxed subprocess with a 180 s CPU budget for all nine instances together. Score (maximize): mean over the instances of cut_weight / published_optimal_cut, where the evaluator recomputes the cut weight from the edge list; 1.0 means reaching the exact optimum everywhere. The spin-glass energy of the couplings J = -weight is sum(weight) - 2 * cut_weight, so a larger cut is a lower energy

sources.locator: Liers, Juenger, Reinelt and Rinaldi (2004) compute exact ground states of Ising spin glasses by branch-and-cut and introduce these toroidal grid instances with Gaussian couplings.

Barahona (1982) shows that the spin-glass ground-state problem is polynomially solvable on two-dimensional lattices without a field and NP-hard in three dimensions and in two dimensions with a field. The instances of this task are periodic in both directions (toroidal, not planar); for the torus, polynomial algorithms are known for integer couplings bounded by a polynomial in the lattice size (Galluccio, Loebl and Vondrak, Math. Program. 90 (2001) 273-290, doi:10.1007/PL00011425).

Biq Mac library: the t2g torus instances (ising_all.tar.gz) and their optimal cut values in Table 10 of biqmaclib.pdf; no licence stated, so the archive is downloaded by the user and not redistributed here.

limitations: The reference values are the optimal cut weights published with the library, obtained by branch-and-cut with no time limit; the task gives a candidate a few minutes of CPU for nine instances, so matching them is hard and the score is budget-dependent.

Planar two-dimensional lattices without a field are polynomially solvable by matching (Barahona 1982), but these instances are toroidal: for graphs on the torus, polynomial algorithms are known when the integer couplings are bounded by a polynomial in the lattice size (Pfaffian enumeration; Galluccio, Loebl and Vondrak 2001, who credit Barahona 1982 for toroidal square lattices). The couplings here are integers up to about 3.8e5, so that method is pseudo-polynomial for these instances. A transfer-matrix dynamic programme over rows solves the three 10x10 instances exactly in seconds and confirms their published optima; it does not scale to 15x15 and 20x20 within the budget, where the task is a test of heuristics.
Only these nine fixed instances are scored: a better score is a better heuristic on them, not a statement about the Edwards-Anderson model in general.
Couplings are the integer-scaled Gaussian weights of the published instances; the evaluator reports the corresponding spin-glass energy but scores the cut weight.

sources.locator: Liers, Juenger, Reinelt and Rinaldi (2004) compute exact ground states of these three-dimensional toroidal Ising spin glasses by branch-and-cut.
Barahona (1982) proves that finding spin-glass ground states on three-dimensional lattices is NP-hard, which is why these instances are hard for heuristics.

Biq Mac library: the t3g torus instances (ising_all.tar.gz) and their optimal cut values in Table 10 of biqmaclib.pdf; no licence stated, so the archive is downloaded by the user and not redistributed here.

limitations: The reference values come from branch-and-cut runs without a time limit; this task gives a few minutes of CPU for nine instances, so the score is budget-dependent and not comparable with exact solvers.

Couplings are the integer-scaled Gaussian weights of the published instances; the evaluator reports the corresponding energy but scores the cut weight.
Ground-state degeneracy is not examined: the task only measures how close the recomputed cut weight comes to the published optimum.

NP-hardness is a worst-case statement and these instances have at most 343 spins: simulated annealing with a few hundred replicas reaches the published optimum of eight of the nine instances within seconds each (the ninth to within 3e-4), so a score close to 1.0 is attainable inside the budget and the headroom of the task is the gap between the seed (0.885) and 1.0.

tasks.name: Software engineering: history-based test prioritisation in continuous integration (ABB IOF/ROL)
tasks.description: Order the test cases of each of the 320 continuous-integration cycles of ABB's IOF/ROL system so that failing tests run early, using only the verdicts of earlier cycles. Each cycle's verdicts are revealed after its order is committed; the score is the mean APFD over cycles with both failing and passing tests.
tasks.contract: prioritize(cycle, history) -> list of int. cycle = {'cycle': int, 'tests': [{'id': int, 'duration': int}, ...]} lists the test cases of one continuous-integration cycle, sorted by id (durations are the data set's approximate run times). history lists every earlier cycle in order as {'cycle': int, 'tests': [{'id', 'duration', 'failed': bool}, ...]}. Return a permutation of the cycle's test ids, the test to run first first. A cycle's verdicts are revealed, by appending it to history, only after its order has been committed. Score: mean APFD over the cycles that contain both failing and passing tests, maximised; APFD = 1 - (sum of the 1-based positions of the m failing tests) / (n m) + 1 / (2 n) for a cycle of n tests, so a random order scores 0.5 in expectation. prioritize() is called once per cycle, all cycles in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 60 s CPU in total, 2 GB); module-level state persists between calls. It should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks); an invalid order makes the evaluation invalid.

sources.locator: Spieker, Gotlieb, Marijan and Mossige (ISSTA 2017): reinforcement learning for test prioritisation and selection in CI; introduces the ABB Paint Control and IOF/ROL data.

Elbaum, Rothermel and Penix (FSE 2014): history-based test prioritisation and selection in continuous integration at Google.
Rothermel, Untch, Chu and Harrold (TSE 2001): test case prioritisation and the APFD metric.

limitations: The verdicts are historical: the order cannot change which tests fail, and every test of a cycle is assumed to run.

Plain APFD with each failing test counted as one fault; the source paper reports NAPFD under a time budget, so its numbers are not directly comparable. Durations are given to the candidate but not used by the metric.
Repeated executions of a test within one cycle are merged (failed if any execution failed); the data set's LastRun and LastResults columns and its row order are not passed on.
Ordering failing tests first gives 0.815 on this data; a last-verdict heuristic (the seed) gives 0.585, and 99 of the 320 cycles contain a single test.
The verdicts are public; embedding them is outside the contract but cannot be checked automatically.

The suite's evaluator template imports the candidate module in the evaluator process before scoring; every scored call runs in the sandbox, which cannot read the held-out data, but deliberately hostile import-time code could. Untrusted evaluations should run in a container without the prepared files.

tasks.name: Software engineering: pairwise covering array for the Apache configuration model
tasks.description: Build a smallest pairwise covering array for the 172-option Apache web-server model of Cohen et al., avoiding its forbidden option combinations. Every feasible pair of option settings must appear in some test configuration; fewer configurations is better.
tasks.contract: generate(model) -> list of rows. model = {'name': str, 'strength': t, 'values': [v_0, ..., v_{k-1}], 'forbidden': [[[p, level], ...], ...]}: parameter p takes a level in 0..v_p-1 and each forbidden entry lists parameter-level pairs that must not all occur in one row. Return a list of rows, each a list of k Python ints. Every row must avoid all forbidden combinations, and the rows together must contain every combination of levels of t distinct parameters that occurs in at least one valid configuration (the evaluator decides feasibility exactly). Score: number of rows, minimised; an array that misses a feasible combination or contains a forbidden one is invalid. generate() runs in a sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; CPU limit 60 s for pairwise and 120 s for 3-way tasks, 2 GB); it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

sources.locator: Cohen, Dwyer and Shi (TSE 2008): constrained interaction testing of highly configurable systems; introduces the SPIN, GCC, Apache and Bugzilla constraint models and a SAT-checked greedy construction.
Jia, Cohen, Harman and Petke (ICSE 2015): hyperheuristic search for constrained covering arrays; publishes the benchmark archive used here.
ICSE15_HHSA_Benchmarks.zip (CC BY 4.0): CASA-format model and constraint files; levels are numbered from 1.
Supplementary table of the FastCA repository: HHSA and CASA sizes (2-way and 3-way, 5-hour cutoff) on the same HHSA-format instance files.

limitations: Published sizes on these exact files: HHSA 30 rows and CASA 32 rows (FastCA repository supplementary table, minimum over runs with a 5-hour cutoff).
The array size is the only objective; generation time is bounded by the sandbox CPU limit and is not scored, whereas the published solvers ran for 1000 s to 5 h in C++.
Feasible combinations are decided by an exact search at preparation time and cross-checked with Z3 in the tests; a Z3 disagreement would change the required set.
The models are public; a candidate could embed a precomputed array. Scores are comparable with published sizes only for arrays generated within the contract.

tasks.name: Software engineering: optimal register coalescing on the 22 largest challenge graphs
tasks.description: Colour the 22 interference graphs with 3,000 to 28,640 nodes from the Appel-George Optimal Coalescing Challenge with 6 registers so that as much move (affinity) weight as possible joins nodes of the same colour. The score is the mean share of affinity weight left uncoalesced; lower is better.
tasks.contract: coalesce(problem) -> list of int. problem = {'name': str, 'nodes': N, 'registers': K (6 in every instance), 'interference': [[i, j], ...], 'affinities': [[i, j, w], ...]} with nodes numbered 0..N-1: nodes 0..K-1 are machine registers and node i < K must get colour i; every other node interferes with fewer than K nodes, so a legal colouring always exists; affinities are move-related pairs with positive integer weights. Return N Python ints in 0..K-1 such that no interference pair shares a colour. Cost of an instance: total weight of the affinity pairs whose two nodes get different colours. Score: mean over the task's instances of cost divided by the instance's total affinity weight (the share of move weight not coalesced), minimised; 0 means every move is coalesced. An illegal colouring of any instance makes the evaluation invalid. coalesce() is called once per instance, all instances in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 120 s CPU in total, 3 GB); it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

sources.locator: Appel and George, Optimal Coalescing Challenge (2000): 474 interference graphs with affinities, problem and solution format, checker and published solution sets.
Appel and George (PLDI 2001): optimal spilling by integer programming followed by coalescing; source of the challenge graphs.
George and Appel (TOPLAS 1996): iterated register coalescing, the heuristic behind the published greedy solution set.
Grund and Hack (CC 2007): cutting-plane ILP for optimal coalescing; their solutions of all 474 challenge instances are on the challenge page.
Park and Moon (TOPLAS 2004): optimistic register coalescing, the basis of the published optimistic solution set.

limitations: Best-known costs are the published Grund-Hack ILP solutions; CPLEX proved 19 of the 22 optimal, while instances 139, 304 and 387 stopped after five minutes. Blazy and Robillard (LCTES 2009) report optimal solutions for these three, which were not checked here.
The score averages per-instance shares of uncoalesced affinity weight; the challenge itself evaluates instances separately, so totals in the literature are not the same number.
All graphs come from one compiler (SML/NJ) with six registers after optimal spilling; methods tuned on them may not transfer to other register files or allocators.
The instances are public; a candidate could embed precomputed colourings, which the contract excludes.
The candidate gets 120 s of CPU time in total in a Python sandbox; published solvers had no comparable limit.

tasks.name: Software engineering: spectrum-based fault localisation of seeded faults in three CPython modules
tasks.description: Rank the code blocks of a faulty module by suspiciousness using only its program spectrum: for each block, how many failing and passing tests execute it. The 532 faults are first-order mutants of textwrap, urllib.parse and fractions; the score is the mean EXAM (rank of the faulty block divided by the number of blocks).
tasks.contract: localize(spectrum) -> list of float. spectrum = {'subject': 'textwrap', 'urllib.parse' or 'fractions', 'blocks': n, 'failed': F, 'passed': P, 'ef': [n ints], 'ep': [n ints]} describes one faulty version of the module: F of its pool tests fail (their outcome differs from the correct module's) and P pass, and ef[b] (ep[b]) is the number of failing (passing) tests that execute block b, where blocks are the evaluator's block probes (function entries, branch outcomes, loop bodies and exits, handlers) in a random order that is drawn anew for every fault and every evaluation, so an index does not denote the same block in different faults or evaluations; the faults are presented in a random order as well. Return n finite numbers, a suspiciousness per block (higher means more likely faulty). Score: mean EXAM over the 532 faults, i.e. the faulty block's rank (ties count as their average rank) divided by n, minimised. localize() is called once per fault, all faults in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 120 s CPU in total, 2 GB); it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

sources.locator: Jones and Harrold (ASE 2005): the Tarantula fault-localisation technique and its evaluation by the share of code examined (the seed).
Abreu, Zoeteweij and van Gemund (TAIC PART 2007): accuracy of spectrum-based fault localisation with block hit spectra; Ochiai coefficient.
Wong, Debroy, Gao and Li (IEEE Trans. Reliability 2014): the DStar formula.
Yoo (SSBSE 2012): evolving risk-evaluation formulas with genetic programming, the program-search setting of this task.
Pearson et al. (ICSE 2017): results on artificial faults do not carry over to real faults; the main caveat of this task.
CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence): textwrap, urllib.parse and fractions.

limitations: Faults are artificial first-order mutants, one per version; Pearson et al. (ICSE 2017) found that rankings of fault-localisation techniques on artificial faults do not predict their rankings on real faults.

Spectra are block hit counts from this evaluator's probes and a seeded 240-call test pool per module, not statement coverage of a project's own test suite; the faulty block is the statement-level block containing the mutated statement (faults on one-line compound statements are left out), so EXAM values are not comparable with published ones.
Undetected mutants and mutants that break the import are excluded; textwrap contributes 110 faults, urllib.parse 183 and fractions 239.

Reference values computed here: Tarantula (the seed) 0.0506, Ochiai 0.0268 and DStar(2) 0.0248 mean EXAM; ranking each faulty block first among blocks with an identical spectrum would give 0.0087, a bound for formulas of the counts that no single formula need reach.

Blocks and faults are shown in a random order that changes with every evaluation, so neither a position nor the number of the call carries information; the score of a formula of the counts does not depend on the order. The faults are public, however: a spectrum identifies its fault, and a search can still overfit this fault set.
provenance.benchmark: Software engineering: spectrum-based fault localisation of seeded faults in three CPython modules
provenance.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

tasks.name: Software engineering: coverage-guided fuzzing of CPython's html.parser
tasks.description: Generate at most 1,000 input strings that drive html.parser.HTMLParser with _markupbase (CPython 3.12.14) through as many code blocks as possible. The score is the number of distinct instrumented blocks (function entries, branch outcomes, loop exits, handlers) that the inputs reach.

tasks.name: Software engineering: log parsing (event template identification) on the 16 Loghub-2k data sets
tasks.description: Group the messages of 16 system logs (2,000 lines each, from HDFS, Hadoop, Spark, Linux, OpenSSH and others) by the log statement that produced them, given only the message texts. The score is the mean grouping accuracy against the corrected ground-truth events.
tasks.contract: parse(dataset) -> list. dataset = {'name': one of Android, Apache, BGL, HDFS, HPC, Hadoop, HealthApp, Linux, Mac, OpenSSH, OpenStack, Proxifier, Spark, Thunderbird, Windows, Zookeeper, 'messages': [2000 str]} gives the message contents of 2,000 log lines of one system in their original order (header fields such as time, level and component already removed). Return one group label (int or str) per message; messages with equal labels are claimed to come from the same log statement (event template). Grouping accuracy of a data set: the share of messages whose group contains exactly the messages of their ground-truth event, no more and no fewer. Score: mean grouping accuracy over the 16 data sets, maximised. parse() is called once per data set, all data sets in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 120 s CPU in total, 2 GB); per-data-set settings are allowed, as in the published benchmarks; it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

tasks.name: Software engineering: loop-invariant inference for the Code2Inv programs
tasks.description: Infer a loop invariant for each of the 124 valid Code2Inv C programs so that Z3 proves initiation, consecution and the post-condition. The procedure may query a verifier that returns counterexamples (50 queries per program); the score is the fraction of programs with a proven invariant.
tasks.contract: synthesize(problem, oracle) -> str. problem = {'name': str, 'c_source': str (declarations, pre-condition assignments, one while loop and a post-condition assert), 'variables': [names of the integer program variables], 'definitions': str (the Code2Inv SMT-LIB definitions of pre-f, trans-f and post-f over the variables, their primed next-state copies and SSA auxiliaries), 'max_queries': 50}. Return a loop invariant as one SMT-LIB Boolean term over the variables using integer literals (write negative numbers as (- n)), true, false and the operators and, or, not, =>, ite, =, <, <=, >, >=, +, -, * (at most one non-constant factor), div and mod (positive literal divisor), i.e. linear integer arithmetic. It is correct when Z3 proves initiation (pre-f implies it), consecution (it and trans-f imply it for the primed variables) and safety (it implies post-f), each within a fixed resource limit. oracle(invariant) performs the same check and returns {'valid': bool, 'failed': 'initiation', 'consecution', 'safety', 'syntax' or a budget message, 'state': a counterexample assignment of the variables or None, 'next': the successor assignment for consecution failures or None, 'queries_left': int, 'error': parse error if any}; each problem allows 50 queries and all queries share a fixed Z3 resource budget. Score: fraction of the 124 valid programs whose returned invariant is correct, maximised; a returned str that does not parse counts as not proven, a non-str answer makes the evaluation invalid. synthesize() is called once per program, all programs in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses, so Z3 is not available there; 180 s CPU in total, 2 GB); it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

sources.locator: Si, Dai, Raghothaman, Naik and Song (NeurIPS 2018): Code2Inv, learning loop invariants with a verifier in the loop; introduces the 133-program benchmark.
Pinned Code2Inv benchmark directory: C programs (C_instances/c) and SMT-LIB verification conditions (C_instances/c_smt2); no licence stated.
Ryan, Wong, Yao, Gu and Jana (ICLR 2020): CLN2INV; removes 9 invalid programs and solves all 124 others (LoopInvGen 104, Code2Inv 90), one hour per problem.
Garg, Loding, Madhusudan and Neider (CAV 2014): ICE learning, invariant inference from a teacher's implication and counterexamples.
Flanagan and Leino (FME 2001): Houdini, the template-based invariant pruning used by the seed.

limitations: Of the 133 programs, bounded model checking here finds 9 whose post-condition can fail (26, 27, 31, 32, 61, 62, 72, 75, 106), the count reported by Ryan et al. (2020); those 9 are excluded, so scores use 124 programs.
Five of the 124 post-conditions hold at every loop exit, so the invariant 'true' already proves them; many others need only simple bounds.

Correctness follows the benchmark's own SMT-LIB verification conditions, checked by Z3 with a fixed resource limit; the C programs themselves are not executed, so an error in an encoding would carry over.

Invariants are restricted to linear integer arithmetic and the candidate has 50 verifier queries per program and 180 s of CPU in total, while published tools had one hour per program and unbounded solver calls (LoopInvGen averaged about 3,600 calls); published counts are therefore not directly comparable.
The programs are public and solved invariants circulate; embedding them is outside the contract but cannot be checked automatically.
Results depend on the Z3 version only where a check reaches the resource limit; this run used z3-solver 5.1.0.

provenance.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

tasks.name: Software engineering: mutation-adequate test generation for CPython's fractions
tasks.description: Generate at most 30 test calls for fractions.Fraction (parsing, arithmetic, rounding, formatting) that distinguish as many of its 453 first-order mutants as possible from the original module. A mutant is killed when some test's result or exception type differs; the score is the fraction killed.
tasks.contract: generate_tests(subject) -> list of tests. subject = {'subject': str, 'files': {path: source} (CPython 3.12.14), 'target': path of the mutated module, 'api': {call: [argument kinds]}, 'mutants': [{'unit', 'operator', 'line', 'start', 'end', 'replacement'}, ...], 'max_tests': 30}. A test is {'call': name, 'args': [values]}. Argument kinds: 'str' (at most 500 characters), 'int' (|n| <= 10000), 'opt_int' (such an int or None), 'bool', 'float' (finite, |x| <= 1e6), 'fraction' (a str of at most 30 characters for Fraction(), with an exponent of at most two digits), 'spec' (a format spec of at most 12 characters without runs of four digits), 'number' (a 'fraction' str, an int with |n| <= 1000 or a float), 'numbers' (a list of at most 40 values, each a 'fraction' str, an int with |n| <= 10000 or a float with |x| <= 1e6), 'pairs' (at most 20 [str, str] pairs of at most 100 characters each), {'options': {keyword: kind}} (keyword arguments), {'strings': n} (exactly n strings), {'choice': [allowed values]}. Calls: textwrap: wrap/fill/shorten(text, width, options) -> textwrap.<call>(text, width, **options), dedent(text), indent(text, prefix); urllib.parse: each call is the function of that name with the arguments in order (urlparse/urlsplit(url, scheme, allow_fragments), urljoin(base, url, allow_fragments), parse_qs/parse_qsl(qs, keep_blank_values, strict_parsing, max_num_fields, separator), quote/quote_plus(string, safe)), urlunparse/urlunsplit get the strings as a tuple, urlencode(pairs, doseq, safe) passes the pairs as tuples; fractions: parse(s) -> Fraction(s), make(n, d) -> Fraction(n, d), from_float(x), binary(a, op, b) applies the operator (or divmod, max) to a and b with str operands converted by Fraction, limit_denominator(s, m), round(s, ndigits) (round(Fraction(s)) when ndigits is None), format(s, spec) -> format(Fraction(s), spec), method(s, name) -> getattr(Fraction(s), name)(); statistics (str values become Fraction): summary(name, data) -> statistics.<name>(data), median_grouped(data, interval), quantiles(data, n, method), weighted(name, data, weights) -> fmean or harmonic_mean with weights, spread_given_center(name, data, c) -> variance/pvariance/stdev/pstdev(data, c), bivariate(name, x, y) -> covariance, correlation (linear or ranked) or linear_regression (proportional or not), normal(mu, sigma, method, x) -> NormalDist(mu, sigma).method(x) (quantiles(int(x)) for 1 <= x <= 1000, overlap(NormalDist(x, 1.0))), from_samples(data). A mutant is the target file with lines start..end replaced by 'replacement'; it is killed when some test's outcome differs from the original module's outcome, where the outcome is a hash of the repr of the result (generators consumed, at most 10,001 items) or the type name of the raised exception. A call is cut off, with the outcome 'timeout', when it exceeds 50,000 steps or its CPU-time limit. A step is a function entry or a loop iteration inside a function of the given files, so the count does not depend on the machine (the largest call the argument bounds allow needs about 10,000 steps). The CPU-time limit is 0.2 s on the original module and 0.2 s plus ten times the original's own CPU time on a mutant; it only matters for calls that spend long inside C code or whose iterations grow ever more expensive. Tests that time out on the original are ignored. Score: killed mutants / all mutants, maximised (equivalent mutants make 1.0 unreachable); the whole mutation analysis may take at most 240 s of CPU time, otherwise the evaluation is invalid. generate_tests() runs in a sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 60 s CPU, 2 GB) and may load the files and mutants itself; it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks). Invalid tests make the evaluation invalid.

sources.locator: Fraser and Zeller (TSE 2012): generating unit tests and oracles that kill mutants.
DeMillo and Offutt (TSE 1991): constraint-based generation of test data that kills mutants.
Lukasczyk, Kroiss and Fraser (EMSE 2023): automated unit test generation for Python (Pynguin), assessed by coverage and mutation score.
Papadakis, Jia, Harman and Le Traon (ICSE 2015): trivial compiler equivalence for removing equivalent mutants.
CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence): the mutated modules.

limitations: Mutants come from this evaluator's operator set (MutPy- and mutmut-style replacements inside function bodies); scores are not comparable with other mutation tools.
Non-compiling, duplicate and trivially compiler-equivalent mutants are removed, but other equivalent mutants remain, so 1.0 is unreachable and the number of killable mutants is unknown.
Oracles are regression oracles: a test kills a mutant when the hash of the result's repr or the exception type differs from the original's, which also counts differences a specification might allow.

Reference computed with this evaluator (Linux x86-64, CPython 3.12): the seed's generate_tests with max_tests = 2000, i.e. 2,000 random calls, kills 239 of the 453 mutants (52.8%); the 30-test budget is this dataset's choice.
The candidate sees the mutants and may run them, so the task measures test generation and selection against known mutants, not generalisation to unseen faults.

Step counting makes the verdict on loops independent of the machine, but CPU-time limits remain as a safety net: a test whose call on the original module needs about 0.2 s of CPU time (very large powers, tab expansion to megabytes or long exact-fraction computations: 9,999 quantiles of 40 fractions need 0.06 s on the machine used for this record) is used or ignored depending on the machine.

tasks.name: Software engineering: programming by example for string transformations (SyGuS-Comp PBE strings)
tasks.description: Write a synthesiser that, from a few input-output examples and a grammar, returns a string-manipulation program (phone numbers, names, initials, university addresses) that also reproduces held-out examples of the same task. The score is the fraction of 27 SyGuS-Comp tasks solved.
tasks.contract: synthesize(task) -> str. task = {'name': str, 'function': str, 'params': [[name, sort], ...], 'sort': 'String', 'start': nonterminal, 'grammar': [[nonterminal, sort, [productions]], ...], 'examples': [[[argument strings], output string], ...]} is a SyGuS PBE string problem: productions are parameter names, literals (string literals as {'str': value}, integers, true, false), other nonterminals or operator lists such as ['str.substr', 'ntString', 'ntInt', 'ntInt']. Return one SMT-LIB term (an S-expression string; string literals in double quotes with "" for a quote, negative numbers as -1 or (- 1)) that the grammar derives from 'start'. Operations follow SMT-LIB 2.6 string semantics (str.++, str.len, str.at, str.substr, str.indexof, str.replace, str.to.int, int.to.str, str.prefixof, str.suffixof, str.contains, +, -, =, ite, with the edge cases of the standard, e.g. out-of-range str.at and str.substr give "" and str.to.int of a non-numeral gives -1). A task is solved when the term reproduces the given examples and the held-out examples of the benchmark's '-long' variant. Score: fraction of the 27 tasks solved, maximised; a term that does not parse or leaves the grammar counts as unsolved, a non-str answer makes the evaluation invalid. synthesize() is called once per task, all tasks in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 120 s CPU in total, 2 GB); it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

sources.locator: Gulwani (POPL 2011): FlashFill, synthesising string transformations in spreadsheets from input-output examples.
Alur et al. (FMCAD 2013): syntax-guided synthesis, the problem format (grammar plus specification) of these tasks.
Alur, Radhakrishna and Udupa (TACAS 2017): EUSolver, enumerative synthesis with divide and conquer, evaluated on SyGuS PBE string tasks.
Padhi, Millstein, Nori and Sharma (CAV 2019): overfitting in synthesis, programs that fit the examples but not the intended function.
Pinned SyGuS benchmarks (no licence stated): the base and '-long' files of the 27 tasks.

limitations: Only 27 tasks, from a few families (11 phone-number tasks, 4 name-combination tasks, 6 university-address tasks and 6 others), so scores move in steps of 1/27 and families are correlated.

Correctness is judged on examples: the given ones plus 8 to 94 held-out examples of the '-long' variant per task (3 to 94 distinct ones, because the long files repeat examples; bikes has 3); a program that agrees on all of them but differs elsewhere counts as solved.

SyGuS-Comp scored consistency with the given examples and solving time, not generalisation, so published solved counts are not comparable; the benchmark repository notes that errors and duplicates may exist.
The bottom-up enumeration seed solves 8 of 27 within its budget; the tasks are public and solutions could be remembered, which the contract excludes but cannot check.

The interpreter implements the SMT-LIB 2.6 string semantics used by SyGuS-Comp 2018 and was cross-checked against Z3 on random terms; a solver with different edge-case semantics could disagree on unusual programs.

tasks.name: Software engineering: test-based repair of the QuixBugs Python programs
tasks.description: Write a general repair procedure that receives a buggy QuixBugs Python program with a few visible tests and returns a patch of at most two statements. A patch counts only when it also passes held-out QuixBugs tests and generated tests whose expected outputs come from the reference fix.
tasks.contract: repair(task) -> str. task = {'name': str, 'entry': str, 'source': str, 'tests': [{'input': [arguments], 'expected': value, 'tolerance': float (only for sqrt)}, ...], 'max_statement_edits': 2}: 'source' is a buggy QuixBugs Python program defining the function 'entry'; 'tests' are its visible tests, at least one of which fails. Return the patched program as a str of at most 20000 characters that differs from 'source' in at most 2 statements (replaced, inserted or deleted statements of the parsed program; formatting and comments do not count). A test passes when entry(*input) returns the expected value after JSON normalisation (generators are consumed into lists, tuples become lists), or a number within 'tolerance' of it, within the test's step limit. A step is one function entry or one loop iteration of the program, counted by the evaluator, so the limit does not depend on the speed of the machine: 2,000,000 steps per test, and 25,000,000 for the test levenshtein('rosettacode', 'raisethysword'), on which the reference fix makes 10,308,990 calls (on every other test the reference fixes need at most 761,717 steps). A CPU-time limit of 10 s plus 2 microseconds per allowed step remains as a safety net for programs whose steps are individually slow. Score: fraction of the 31 programs whose patch passes its visible tests, its remaining QuixBugs tests and 10 to 40 generated held-out tests whose expected values come from the reference fix (higher is better); a patch passing only some of them counts as overfitting, not repaired. repair() runs once per program in a sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 4 s CPU, 1 GB) and may execute the given program and tests itself; it should be deterministic. The procedure must be general: remembered program-specific fixes are outside the contract. A repair() call that raises, exceeds its limits or returns something other than a str of at most 20000 characters makes the whole evaluation invalid.

sources.locator: Lin, Koppel, Chen and Solar-Lezama (SPLASH Companion 2017): the QuixBugs benchmark of 40 programs with one-line bugs in Python and Java.
Pinned QuixBugs commit (MIT licence): python_programs, correct_python_programs (used only at preparation time) and json_testcases.
Le Goues, Nguyen, Forrest and Weimer (TSE 2012): GenProg, test-suite-based generate-and-validate repair.
Smith, Barr, Le Goues and Brun (ESEC/FSE 2015): patches that pass the repair tests but fail held-out tests (overfitting).
Ye, Martinez, Durieux and Monperrus (JSS 2021): repair tools on QuixBugs; plausible patches checked for overfitting with generated tests.

limitations: Uses the 31 Python programs with JSON tests; the nine graph programs are excluded, so results reported on all 40 programs are not comparable, nor are results of tools that call language models.

Correctness is decided by tests: the visible tests, the remaining QuixBugs tests and 10 to 40 generated inputs per program checked against the reference fix. A semantically different but test-equivalent patch counts as a repair, and a wrong patch that agrees on all these inputs would also count; there is no manual patch review.
Generated inputs respect the documented preconditions and avoid inputs whose correct output is not unique; inputs on which the reference fix itself loops (some wrap cases) are excluded.
The programs and their fixes are public, so a candidate could embed remembered fixes; the contract excludes this but it cannot be checked automatically.
Each repair() call gets 4 s of CPU time in a Python sandbox, far less than the hours given to repair tools in the literature.

The suite's evaluator template imports the candidate module in the evaluator process before scoring; every scored call runs in the sandbox, which cannot read the held-out data, but deliberately hostile import-time code could. Untrusted evaluations should run in a container without the prepared files.
