tasks.name: Software engineering: superoptimisation of the 25 Hacker's Delight kernels
tasks.description: Rewrite each of 25 bit-manipulation kernels (Hacker's Delight, as used by Brahma and STOKE) into the shortest straight-line program over 32-bit operations that Z3 proves equal to the reference for every input. The score is the total instruction count; unproven programs count at the reference length.
tasks.contract: optimize(problem) -> list of instructions. problem = {'name': str, 'description': str, 'inputs': [names], 'reference': [[dest, op, arg, ...], ...], 'operations': {op: arity}, 'max_instructions': 64}. An instruction [dest, op, args...] defines a new name; arguments are input names, earlier destinations or integer constants in [-2^31, 2^32 - 1] (taken modulo 2^32); the value of the last instruction is the result. All values are 32-bit words: add, sub, mul, and, or, xor, not, neg wrap modulo 2^32; shl, lshr and ashr take the full word as shift amount (32 or more gives 0, or the sign fill for ashr); udiv, urem, sdiv and srem follow SMT-LIB (x udiv 0 = 2^32 - 1, x urem 0 = x, x sdiv 0 = 1 for negative x and 2^32 - 1 otherwise, x srem 0 = x); eq, ne, ult, ule, ugt, uge, slt, sle, sgt, sge give 1 or 0; select(c, a, b) gives a if c != 0 else b. Score: total number of instructions over the 25 kernels, minimised; a kernel's program counts only if it agrees with the reference on 300 test inputs and Z3 proves it equal to the reference for every input within a fixed resource limit, otherwise the reference's length counts. A structurally invalid program (unknown operation, wrong arity, undefined or reused name, more than 64 instructions) makes the evaluation invalid. optimize() is called once per kernel, all kernels in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 120 s CPU in total, 2 GB); it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

sources.locator: Massalin (ASPLOS 1987): the superoptimizer, an exhaustive search for the shortest instruction sequence computing a function.
Gulwani, Jha, Tiwari and Venkatesan (PLDI 2011): synthesis of loop-free programs; defines the 25 Hacker's Delight benchmarks P1-P25.
Schkufza, Sharma and Aiken (ASPLOS 2013): stochastic superoptimization (STOKE), evaluated on the same 25 kernels.
STOKE's straight-line C versions of p01-p25 (Apache-2.0); the reference programs are parsed from these files, with p12, p13, p20 and p24 corrected.
Phothilimthana, Thakur, Bodik and Dhurjati (ASPLOS 2016): scaling up superoptimization with an enumerative and stochastic search.

limitations: The 32-bit instruction set with unit costs is this dataset's choice; STOKE optimises x86-64 code for latency and Brahma synthesises from given component multisets, so published program sizes are not directly comparable.

STOKE's C files for p12, p13, p20 and p24 compute other functions than the named kernels (operand swap, signed instead of unsigned shift or division, and a wrong final operand); these four were corrected, and all 25 references were checked against independent Python specifications and against the clang-compiled corrected C on 100,000 inputs.
C's undefined cases (division by zero in p20 at x = 0, shifts by 32 or more in p19) follow SMT-LIB semantics, so equivalence is required on those inputs too.

A program counts only if Z3 proves equivalence within a fixed resource limit; a correct program whose proof exceeds the limit counts at the reference length. Proofs for all programs tried here took well under a second.

The reference total is 135 instructions; minimal lengths in this instruction set are unknown. Shorter verified programs exist (for example 3 instead of 10 instructions for the power-of-two test), so the reference is not the state of the art.
The kernels are public and textbook solutions are well known; returning remembered programs is allowed by the score but the contract asks for a search procedure.

tasks.name: Long paths above the random-graph phase transition

tasks.name: Snake-in-the-box in the 10-cube
tasks.description: Construct a snake that is as long as possible in the hypercube Q_10: the graph whose vertices are the integers 0 to 2^10 - 1, two of them adjacent when they differ in exactly one bit. A snake is an induced path: consecutive vertices of the path are adjacent, and no two vertices that are not consecutive on it are adjacent.
tasks.contract: construct() -> list of at least two distinct integers in [0, 2**10): the vertices of the path in order. Consecutive vertices must differ in exactly one bit, and any two non-consecutive ones in at least two bits. Score: number of edges of the path (the number of vertices minus one), maximized.

tasks.name: Sorting network on 19 inputs
tasks.description: Construct a sorting network on 19 wires with as few comparators as possible. A comparator (i, j) with i < j compares the values on wires i and j and puts the smaller one on wire i and the larger one on wire j; the comparators are applied in the given order. The network must sort every input, that is, leave the values in non-decreasing order along wires 0 to 18.
tasks.contract: construct() -> list of comparators (i, j) with 0 <= i < j < 19, in the order in which they are applied (at least one). The network is verified on all 2^19 inputs of zeros and ones, which is equivalent to sorting every input. Score: number of comparators, minimized (the depth is not scored).

sources.locator: Using Symmetry and Evolutionary Search to Minimize Sorting Networks
Codish et al. (2015), Sorting Networks: to the End and Back Again: new networks for 17 to 20 inputs, mainly about depth (layers), so not evidence for the size objective.
Ehlers and Mueller (2014), Faster Sorting Networks for 17, 19 and 20 Inputs: depth upper bounds, not size.
Depth-13 Sorting Networks for 28 Channels (2025): depth upper bounds for 27 and 28 inputs, not size.

limitations: Exact 0-1 verification over all 2^19 inputs, in blocks of 2^24.
SorterHunter and symmetry-based searches have worked on these sizes for years.

A comparator (i, j) with i < j compares the values on wires i and j and puts the smaller one on wire i and the larger one on wire j; the comparators are applied in the given order. The network must sort every input, that is, leave the values in non-decreasing order along wires 0 to 21.
tasks.contract: construct() -> list of comparators (i, j) with 0 <= i < j < 22, in the order in which they are applied (at least one). The network is verified on all 2^22 inputs of zeros and ones, which is equivalent to sorting every input. Score: number of comparators, minimized (the depth is not scored).

sources.locator: Using Symmetry and Evolutionary Search to Minimize Sorting Networks
Codish et al. (2015), Sorting Networks: to the End and Back Again: new networks for 17 to 20 inputs, mainly about depth (layers), so not evidence for the size objective.
Ehlers and Mueller (2014), Faster Sorting Networks for 17, 19 and 20 Inputs: depth upper bounds, not size.
Depth-13 Sorting Networks for 28 Channels (2025): depth upper bounds for 27 and 28 inputs, not size.

limitations: Exact 0-1 verification over all 2^22 inputs, in blocks of 2^24.
SorterHunter and symmetry-based searches have worked on these sizes for years.
The record was reproduced by this task's verifier from a published solution (or an optimiser run). See VALIDITY.md.

tasks.name: Spherical code, 100 points in dimension 3
tasks.description: Place 100 points on the unit sphere in R^3 so that the smallest angle between two of them is as large as possible (the Tammes problem). The angle between two points is the angle at the centre of the sphere, the arccosine of the inner product of the two unit vectors.
tasks.contract: construct() -> array of shape (100, 3): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid). Score: smallest angle between two points in degrees, maximized.

sources.locator: Henry Cohn, Table of spherical codes (data set; the current table is at https://spherical-codes.org): dimension 3, 100 points
Sloane's tables of 1994-96, dimension 3, 100 points: the source of the first version of this task, kept for comparison
The densest packing of equal circles on a sphere
The closest packing of equal circles on a sphere
Wang, Finding and investigating exact spherical codes: the preprint of the paper cited above, the version that was read.
Musin and Tarasov (2012), The Strong Thirteen Spheres Problem: solves the Tammes problem for n = 13 in R^3 (the main suite task math-tammes-sphere-13-points uses it); not an n of this family.
Musin and Tarasov (2015), The Tammes Problem for N = 14: computer-assisted proof for n = 14 in R^3; the family starts at n = 16.
mt0-svg (2026), The Tammes problem for fifteen points: a preprint, not peer reviewed, on whose strength Cohn's table marks n = 15 in R^3 as optimal; that size has no task for this reason.
Bachoc and Vallentin, Optimality and uniqueness of the (4,10,1/6) spherical code: semidefinite-programming proof for 10 points in R^4; the family starts at n = 11 there.

Leijenhorst (2025), On the computation of three and four-point bounds in discrete geometry and analytic number theory (doctoral thesis, TU Delft): cited by Cohn's table for the optimality of 12 points in R^4, a size the family leaves out for this reason.

Cohn and Kumar (2007), Universally optimal distribution of points on spheres: proves optimality of special codes such as the 600-cell (4, 120) and the 5-dimensional 16-point code, which the family leaves out.

limitations: The listed code is the best known one, found by computer search and not proven optimal (sizes that are proven have no task).
The table is updated all the time: codes of this family were improved in 2022 to 2026. The record is the state on 2026-11-15 and will fall behind.
A result counts as an improvement only above the record by more than 1e-5 degrees, a margin against numerical slack in the listed coordinates.
The record was reproduced by this task's verifier from a published solution (or an optimiser run). See VALIDITY.md.

tasks.contract: construct() -> array of shape (48, 3): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid). Score: smallest angle between two points in degrees, maximized.

sources.locator: Henry Cohn, Table of spherical codes (data set; the current table is at https://spherical-codes.org): dimension 3, 48 points
Sloane's tables of 1994-96, dimension 3, 48 points: the source of the first version of this task, kept for comparison
The densest packing of equal circles on a sphere
The closest packing of equal circles on a sphere
Wang, Finding and investigating exact spherical codes: the preprint of the paper cited above, the version that was read.
Musin and Tarasov (2012), The Strong Thirteen Spheres Problem: solves the Tammes problem for n = 13 in R^3 (the main suite task math-tammes-sphere-13-points uses it); not an n of this family.
Musin and Tarasov (2015), The Tammes Problem for N = 14: computer-assisted proof for n = 14 in R^3; the family starts at n = 16.
mt0-svg (2026), The Tammes problem for fifteen points: a preprint, not peer reviewed, on whose strength Cohn's table marks n = 15 in R^3 as optimal; that size has no task for this reason.
Bachoc and Vallentin, Optimality and uniqueness of the (4,10,1/6) spherical code: semidefinite-programming proof for 10 points in R^4; the family starts at n = 11 there.

Leijenhorst (2025), On the computation of three and four-point bounds in discrete geometry and analytic number theory (doctoral thesis, TU Delft): cited by Cohn's table for the optimality of 12 points in R^4, a size the family leaves out for this reason.

tasks.contract: construct() -> array of shape (81, 4): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid). Score: smallest angle between two points in degrees, maximized.

sources.locator: Henry Cohn, Table of spherical codes (data set; the current table is at https://spherical-codes.org): dimension 4, 81 points
Sloane's tables of 1994-96, dimension 4, 81 points: the source of the first version of this task, kept for comparison

tasks.contract: construct() -> array of shape (56, 5): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid). Score: smallest angle between two points in degrees, maximized.

sources.locator: Henry Cohn, Table of spherical codes (data set; the current table is at https://spherical-codes.org): dimension 5, 56 points
Sloane's tables of 1994-96, dimension 5, 56 points: the source of the first version of this task, kept for comparison

tasks.name: TDC ADMET AMES
tasks.description: Predict whether a compound is mutagenic in the Ames test (1) or not (0) from its molecular structure, given as a SMILES string (endpoint AMES of the Therapeutics Data Commons ADMET benchmark group). The measured compounds are split by molecular scaffold into a training, a validation and a test part. The test part is fixed; the candidate is run five times (seeds 1 to 5), each time with a different division of the other compounds into training and validation. It receives the training and validation compounds with their values and the test compounds without, and returns one prediction per test compound. Each of the five runs is a separate process that receives only these arguments: it cannot read the evaluator's files, start other processes or open network connections, and it has 700 seconds. The score is the area under the ROC curve on the test compounds, averaged over the five runs; higher is better.
tasks.contract: fit_predict(train_smiles, train_y, valid_smiles, valid_y, test_smiles, info) -> sequence of finite numbers, one per test molecule in the given order: a score that is larger for class 1 (for example its probability). train_smiles, valid_smiles and test_smiles are lists of SMILES strings, train_y and valid_y lists of numbers; info has name, metric, kind ('regression' or 'binary') and seed. Score: mean over the seeds 1 to 5 of the area under the ROC curve on the test part, maximized.

sources.locator: AMES
In silico Prediction of Chemical Ames Mutagenicity
Ames Mutagenicity: binary classification, 7,255 drugs, reference Xu et al. 2012.

Huang et al. (2022), Artificial intelligence foundation for therapeutic science (Nat Chem Biol): the Therapeutics Data Commons paper linked from the TDC site, benchmark paper only; also arXiv 2102.09548, Therapeutics Data Commons: Machine Learning Datasets and Tasks for Drug Discovery and Development.

limitations: Leaders are large tuned ensembles or foundation-model fine-tunes.
Needs PyTDC and rdkit: not in .venv-tasks, so the evaluator restarts itself under tools/venv-admet (created by the README's setup steps).

Every scoring call of the candidate runs in the main suite's sandbox (a child process with an audit hook, 700 s and 6 GB for one call): it keeps a search from coming across the test labels and is not a security boundary against a candidate written to attack the evaluator.
The record was found in a hashed snapshot of its source; it is not replayed. See VALIDITY.md.

tasks.name: Thomson problem, N = 10
tasks.description: Place 10 equal point charges on the unit sphere in R^3 so that their Coulomb energy, the sum of 1/distance over all pairs of points, is as small as possible (the Thomson problem).
tasks.contract: construct() -> array of shape (10, 3): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid, and so are two points that coincide). Score: sum over all pairs of points of 1/(Euclidean distance), minimized.

sources.locator: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere
Structure and dynamics of spherical crystals characterized for the Thomson problem
Defect motifs for spherical topologies
Cambridge Cluster Database, global minima for the Thomson problem (N, energy, point group, coordinates), with updates from W. Deeter's site.
J. J. Thomson (1904), On the structure of the atom: the corpuscle model that gave the problem its name (rings of corpuscles in a charged sphere; the surface problem is the later idealisation).
Schwartz (2013), The Five-Electron Case of Thomson's Problem: computer-assisted proof for N = 5; outside the N range of this family.
Erber and Hockney (1997), Complex Systems: Equilibrium Configurations of N Equal Charges on a Sphere (2 <= N <= 112), Adv. Chem. Phys.: extended tables.

limitations: Only N = 2 to 6 and N = 12 have a published rigorous proof (a proof for N = 7 was announced in 2026 and is not peer reviewed); the other energies are putative minima that many groups have optimised for decades, so matching is the likely outcome.
The record has 9 decimals; a result counts as an improvement only below it by more than 1e-8.
The record was reproduced by this task's verifier from a published solution (or an optimiser run). See VALIDITY.md.

tasks.contract: construct() -> array of shape (175, 3): one point per row (the verifier scales every row to unit length; a zero or non-finite row is invalid, and so are two points that coincide). Score: sum over all pairs of points of 1/(Euclidean distance), minimized.

sources.locator: Equilibrium configurations of N equal charges on a sphere
Structure and dynamics of spherical crystals characterized for the Thomson problem
Defect motifs for spherical topologies
Cambridge Cluster Database, global minima for the Thomson problem (N, energy, point group, coordinates), with updates from W. Deeter's site.
J. J. Thomson (1904), On the structure of the atom: the corpuscle model that gave the problem its name (rings of corpuscles in a charged sphere; the surface problem is the later idealisation).
Schwartz (2013), The Five-Electron Case of Thomson's Problem: computer-assisted proof for N = 5; outside the N range of this family.
Erber and Hockney (1997), Complex Systems: Equilibrium Configurations of N Equal Charges on a Sphere (2 <= N <= 112), Adv. Chem. Phys.: extended tables.

limitations: Only N = 2 to 6 and N = 12 have a published rigorous proof (a proof for N = 7 was announced in 2026 and is not peer reviewed); the other energies are putative minima that many groups have optimised for decades, so matching is the likely outcome.
The record has 9 decimals; a result counts as an improvement only below it by more than 1e-8.
